en: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent.

Regarding that, they ask: 'What was that non-existence? It was indeed the seers (*ṛṣi*) who existed then as the existent. Regarding that, they ask: 'Who were those seers? The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the seers; for it was they who, prior to all this, desired this [world] through exertion."

They perished through austerity; therefore they are called *ṛṣis*. He kindled [the fire] with his mind and senses; because he kindled (*aindhat*), therefore he is called *indhana*. Indeed, he is *Indha*. Now, that which is the vital breath in the middle—
This very one is Indra; they do not call him "Indra" directly (*parokṣam*), for the gods love the indirect. These, having been kindled, created seven different persons.
They said, "In this state, we shall not be able to procreate; let us combine these seven persons into one."
"Let us make a person," they said; so they made those seven persons into one person.
That which was above the navel, they joined together as two; that which was below the navel, they made into two wings—the person, the person; and there was one person as the foundation. 6.1.1 [4]

Then, that which was the glory (*śrī*) of these seven persons, their essence (*rasa*), they gathered upward; that became his head. Because they gathered his glory upward, it is called "head" (*śiras*). Upon that very thing, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) took their support.

Therefore, this became the head; and because the vital breaths (prāṇas) took refuge there, they became the two shoulders; and because they took refuge in the whole, it became the body. That very person became Prajāpati.
That person who was Prajāpati is indeed this very fire-altar that is being built.
He consists of seven persons.
For this person consists of seven persons: four are the self and three are the wings and tail.
Indeed, of that person, four are the self and three are the wings and tail. Now, insofar as he increases the self by one person, by that vigor this self raises up the wings and tail. 6.1.1 [7]
Now, as for the fire which is deposited on the built altar:
whatever prosperity and whatever essence belongs to these seven persons, that they now carry upward together; that is his head, and in it all the gods are supported, for it is here.
They offer oblations to all the gods; therefore, this indeed is the head.
This Puruṣa, Prajāpati, desired, "May I become more, may I procreate. He exerted himself and practiced austerity.
Having exerted himself and practiced austerity, he first created Brahman itself—the threefold knowledge. That [knowledge] was for him.

Therefore, it became his foundation; hence they say, "Brahman is the foundation of all this. Therefore, after reciting [the Veda], one finds a firm footing, for this Brahman is indeed the foundation. Established upon that foundation, he performed austerity. 6.1.1 [9] He created the waters.

From the world of speech itself, speech was created as his [portion]; it pervaded all this, whatever there is. Because it pervaded (*āp*), therefore it is called *āpaḥ*; because it chose (*vṛ*) [it], therefore it is called *vāk*. 6.1.1. He desired.

"May I be born from these waters," he thought; he entered the waters together with this triple knowledge (the three Vedas). From that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "Let there be! "Let there be more! he said.
Then Brahman itself was first created—the triple knowledge. Therefore they say, "Brahman is his [head]."
For it is said that "the first-born of all"; therefore, from that Puruṣa, Brahman alone was created first.
That [Brahman] was created as his very mouth. Therefore, they say of one who has studied the Vedas (anūcāna) that he is like Agni, for this Brahman is indeed the mouth of Agni. 6.1.1 [11]

Then, that embryo which was within was created as Agni. Because he was created as the beginning (*agra*) of all this, therefore he is Agni; for "Agni" is indeed his secret name (*parokṣa*), since the gods are fond of the secret. And then...

When the tear was shed, it became the *aśru* (tear); they call it "horse" (*aśva*) cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. Then that which was like foam became the donkey (*rāsabha*). Then that essence which was smeared on the potsherd became the goat (*aja*). And that which was the potsherd became the earth. 6.1.1. [12]
He desired:
"May I produce from these [waters] this [earth], which is fit for eating. He compressed it and cast it into the waters. That essence of hers which flowed away became the tortoise. Then...
That which is sprinkled upwards—namely, that which is born from above the waters—all this followed after those very waters;
thus, this was seen as a single form alone: water indeed. 6.1.1 [13] He desired.

"May there be more; may it be produced," he thought. He exerted himself; he practiced austerity. Having exerted himself and practiced austerity, he emitted froth. He realized, "This form is indeed something else; it becomes more abundant when one exerts oneself. Having exerted himself and practiced austerity, he [emitted] clay, dried cow-dung, saline soil, sand, gravel, stone, and iron.
He created gold, the plants, and the trees; with that he covered this earth. These, indeed, are the nine creations.
This [earth] was created; therefore they say, "Agni is threefold," for this [earth] is Agni, and because of her...
Every fire-altar is built [with this thought]:
"This [earth] has indeed become a foundation.
It became the earth; he spread it out, and it became the Pṛthivī (the broad one). This is that very [earth].

Thinking herself to be everything in its entirety, she sang; because she sang (*agāyat*), therefore she is the *gāyatrī*. Moreover, they say: "On her back, Agni himself, thinking himself to be everything in its entirety, sang; because he sang, therefore Agni is *gāyatra*.
Therefore, indeed, whoever thinks himself to be everything in its entirety either sings, or delights in singing, or in what has been sung.
That Prajāpati desired:
"May I become more, may I procreate. He united with the earth as his female counterpart through Agni;
from that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "May it thrive! "May it thrive further," [he said].
"So be it," he said.
That embryo which was within was emitted as Vāyu; and those tears that had been shed became these [worlds].
The birds came into being; then that essence which was smeared upon the skull became the Marīcis;
then that which was the skull became the intermediate space (antarikṣa). He desired: "May I be many."

"May there be more; may I procreate. He entered into union with the atmosphere as his mate through the wind. From that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "Bear glory! Thereupon, yonder sun was emitted. This, indeed, is glory. Now, that tear which had flowed forth became the speckled stone (*aśmā pṛśni*). For a tear, indeed, is...
They call it "Tamaśma" cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic; then the essence that was smeared upon the potsherd became the rays, and that which was the potsherd became the sky.
He desired: "May I be many."
"May there be more; may I procreate," he thought. He entered into union with the sun as his mate, the sky.
From that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "Bear the seed. From that, the moon was created. This indeed is the seed.
Now, that which had flowed out as tears became the stars. And that essence which was smeared upon the shell—
The intermediate directions became those [spaces]; then that which was the skull-bowl became the quarters.
Having created these worlds, he desired:
"May I create those offspring who would belong to me in these worlds."
He entered into union with speech by means of the mind.
He became pregnant with eight drops; those were created as the eight Vasus, and he placed them upon this [earth]. 6.1.2. [7]
By means of the mind alone, he entered into union with Speech. He became eleven drops within his womb;
from them the eleven Rudras were created. He placed them in the intermediate space. 6.1.2. [8]
By means of the mind alone, he entered into union with Speech; she became pregnant with twelve drops, and those were born as the twelve Ādityas; he placed them in the sky. 6.1.2. [9]
By means of the mind alone, he entered into union with speech; he became pregnant and created all the gods; he placed them within the quarters. 6.1.2. [10]

Now they say: "When Agni had been created, the Vasus followed after him; he placed them upon this earth. The Rudras [followed] Vāyu; he placed them in the intermediate space. The Ādityas [followed] Āditya; he placed them in the sky. The Viśve Devas [followed] Candramas;
he placed them in the quarters. 6.1.2. [11]
Now they say: Prajāpati, having created these worlds, established himself upon the earth;

for him these plants ripened as food. He ate that, and he became pregnant. From his upward vital breaths (prāṇas) he created the gods, and from those downward vital breaths he created mortal creatures. Therefore, in whatever manner he created at first, in that same manner he created.

Prajāpati indeed created all this, whatever exists here. Having created living beings and having run the entire race, he became exhausted; therefore, indeed, whoever runs the entire race becomes exhausted.

It fell away; from that which had fallen away, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departed from the middle. When it had departed, the gods abandoned him. 6.1.2. [13] He said to Agni: "Unite me. [Agni asked: "What will be mine from that? [He replied: "They shall acknowledge you as me."

"Indeed, one prospers through sons; therefore they speak of a father, a grandfather, a son, and a grandson. Let them speak of me through you; now, do you join me together. "So be it," said Agni, and he joined him together. Therefore, although he is Prajāpati, they call him Agni; indeed, through him they speak of a father, a grandfather, a son, and a grandson.

He who knows thus—[6.1.2.14]—he said to him: "In what shall I place you? He replied, "In the *hita* (the beneficial). Now, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *hita*, for the vital breath is the beneficial.
It is beneficial for all beings; because he placed it as something beneficial (*hita*), therefore one says, "I shall place" (*upadhāsyāmi*) and "I am placing" (*upadadhāmi*).
Regarding this they say: "What is the *hita*? What is the *upahita*? Breath (*prāṇa*) is the *hita*, and speech (*vāk*) is the *upahita*; for upon breath this [speech] rests.
Speech alone was placed upon it; breath indeed was the placement, for these limbs are placed upon breath.
This altar of his was to be piled up (*citya*), for it was to be piled up (*cetavya*); therefore it is called *citya*. And this altar of the sacrificer is likewise to be piled up.
For it is indeed to be piled for him; therefore, it is called *citya*.
These, then, are his five bodies that fell apart: hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow; these are they.

There are five layers; thus, when he piles five layers, he piles him with these very bodies. Because he piles (cinoti), they are called layers (citayaḥ). 6.1.2. [18] Now, that Prajāpati who fell apart—

That year is he; and those five bodies of his which fell apart are the seasons, for there are five seasons. These layers (citayas) are five; thus, when he piles up five layers, he piles him up by means of the seasons. Because he piles them up, they are called layers (citayas). 6.1.2. [19]
That Prajāpati, who was the year, became relaxed;
he is this very wind that blows here. And those five bodies of his which became relaxed were the quarters, for there are indeed five quarters.

These are the five layers; thus, when he piles the five layers, he piles him by means of the quarters. Because he piles them, they are called "layers" (citayaḥ). Now, that fire which is placed upon the piled altar—
That is yonder sun; he is this very same piled fire-altar. This much indeed was that when Agni restored him.
Furthermore, they say: Prajāpati, having been shattered, said to the gods, "Restore me! Those gods—

They said to Agni, "Let us heal this Prajāpati, your father. He replied, "I shall indeed take charge of all this. They said, "So be it. Therefore, although he is Prajāpati, they call him Agni. 6.1.2. [22]
The gods treated him with oblations in the fire;
whichever oblation they offered, that very one, having become a baked brick, returned to him.

Since they originated from what was sacrificed (*iṣṭa*), therefore they are bricks (*iṣṭakā*); therefore, people bake the bricks with fire; they thereby make them into oblations (*āhuti*). He said: "In whatever measure you offer, in that same measure my body becomes. Thus, when he has sacrificed for him...
"From that, the bricks [arose] as the realm of desire.
Regarding this, Aitakṣya used to say:
"Only he who knows the bricks that possess sacrificial formulas (*yajuṣmatī*) and those that are 'become' (*bhūvasī*) would truly know Agni."
"He should pile it up even further; thus he heals his father Prajāpati," so [it is said].
Now, Tāṇḍya used to say:
"The *iṣṭakās* with sacrificial formulas (*yajuṣmatya*) are indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the *lokampṛṇā*s are the common people (*viś*). The eater is indeed..."

The Kṣatriya is food, and where the food of the eater becomes more abundant, that kingdom becomes prosperous and thrives; therefore, one should lay down even more Lokampṛṇā bricks. This is the word of those two, but there is indeed another established rule beyond this. 6.1.2. [26]
He is this father and son:

in that he emitted Agni, by that he is the father of Agni; in that Agni restored him, by that Agni is his father; in that he emitted the gods, by that he is the father of the gods; in that [he emitted] this...
The gods established it for him; the gods are his fathers.
This becomes both:
he is both father and son, and Prajāpati and Agni, and Agni and Prajāpati.
"Prajāpati and the gods, and Prajāpati—he who knows thus. He places it with the formula:
"By that deity. That deity is indeed speech. "In the manner of Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras is indeed breath. "Firmly."
"Sit thou firm," he says; that is to say, "sit thou steady. Or rather, "sit thou firmly established. Verily, by means of speech and breath he thus builds him up;

for Agni is speech and Indra is breath, and Agni belongs to Indra and Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much does he thus build him up. Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods; [Agni] is possessed of all the deities.
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus builds him up.

Regarding this they say: "Why is Agni built upon this [earth]? Because when that deity fell apart, she flowed along this very earth with her essence; and when the gods restored him, they did so from out of this very [earth].
They brought it together; this [central brick] is indeed one and the same, for this [earth] is Agni, since the whole of Agni is built upon her.
And she is four-cornered, for the quarters are her corners; therefore the bricks have four corners, for all the bricks follow the pattern of this one. 6.1.2. [30]

Regarding this they say: "If it is thus one-brick, then how is it five-bricks? Well, this first brick made of clay is indeed the first; whatever else made of clay he places here, that is all just that one brick.
Then, when he places the heads of the animals, that is the animal-brick. And when he places the gold plate and the man, [that is another].
In that he sprinkles with fragments of gold, that is the golden brick;
then, in that he places down the two offering-spoons, the mortar and pestle, and the fuel-sticks, that is the wooden brick;
then, in that he places down the lotus leaf, the tortoise, the curds, the honey, the clarified butter, and whatever else—
And he places food upon it; that very fifth brick is food. Thus, [the altar] consists of five bricks.
6.1.2. Regarding this they say: "Which part is the head of the brick? Some say, "It is that part which one touches while reciting the *yajus*.
He should indeed recite the *yajus* while touching the upper half of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; thus, all these [bricks] of his become so.
"One should not do so because these *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks are repeated; for these bricks are his limbs and joints.

Just as one would cause a fracture in every limb and at every joint, so it would be. Rather, that very place where the fire is finally deposited when piled is the head of all these [bricks]. 6.1.2. [32]
Regarding this they say: "How many animals are placed upon the fire-altar? One should indeed say, "Five," for he places these five animals there. Or else, one should say, "One."
This earth is indeed *aviri*; for by this [earth] all these creatures (*prajā*) are protected (*avati*).
Or rather, this is Agni; for upon her the entire fire-altar (*agni*) is built. Therefore, one should say, "One.
Or else, one should say, "Two."

"This earth" (avī) means both this [earth] and that [heaven]; for these all creatures go (avanti) to them, since this [earth] is clay and that [heaven] is water; thus they become bricks of clay and water. Therefore, one should say "avī," or else one should say "gauḥ" (cow).
"These worlds indeed are *gauḥ* (the cow), for whatever she moves toward, she moves toward these worlds;
these worlds are this piled fire-altar. Therefore, one should say, 'It is *gauḥ*.
Regarding this, they say: "For what desire is the fire-altar piled? "May he become a *suparṇa* (eagle) and carry me to heaven," so says some.
They say: "One should not understand it thus. For having assumed this form, the vital breaths became Prajāpati;

having assumed this form, Prajāpati created the gods; having assumed this form, the gods became immortal. Whatever the vital breaths became by means of this, whatever Prajāpati [became], and whatever the gods [became], that very thing one becomes by means of this. 6.1.3. [1]
In the beginning, this universe was indeed Prajāpati alone. He desired, "May I exist; may I be reproduced. He exerted himself and practiced austerity.
From him, as he exerted himself and practiced austerity, the waters were emitted. Therefore, from a person who has practiced austerity, water is produced. 6.1.3. [2]
The waters said, "Where shall we be? He said, "Perform austerity! They performed austerity;
they emitted foam. Therefore, foam is produced from heated water. The foam said:

"Where am I? Where are you? "Perform austerity," he said. He performed austerity. He created clay. This indeed is what undergoes austerity when it bubbles up and floats in the waters; when it is struck, it becomes nothing but clay. 6.1.3 [4]
The clay said, "Where am I? Where are you? "Heat yourself! he replied. It heated itself and produced sand.
This is why clay is heated when they plow it; therefore, even if they plow very finely, it remains as if sandy.
"This much indeed is what happens: 'Where shall I be? and 'Where shall you be?
6.1.3.[5] From the sand he created gravel;
therefore, sand ultimately becomes gravel, and from gravel...

From that [stone], the *carkarāśman* (the grinding-stone) was produced; therefore, it is stone even to the very end. From stone comes iron; therefore, they smelt iron from stone. From iron comes gold; therefore, iron that has been smelted many times becomes as if it possesses the luster of gold. 6.1.3. [6] Now, because it was emitted (*asṛjyata*), it flowed forth (*akṣarat*); and because it flowed forth, it is called the "syllable" (*akṣara*). And because it did so eight times...
That very [syllable], as it flowed forth, became the eight-syllabled Gāyatrī.
"This has indeed become the foundation," [he thought]; thus it became the *bhūmi* (the earth), and he spread it out. It [became] that.

The earth came into being; upon this earth as a foundation, the beings and the representative of the beings consecrated themselves for the year. The representative of the beings was the *gṛhapati*, and the Dawn was the wife. 6.1.3 [8] Now, those who were those beings...
The seasons are those; and he who is the Lord of Beings (*bhūtānām patiḥ*) is the year (*saṃvatsara*).
And she who is the Dawn (*uṣas*), his wife, is the Dawn (*auṣasī*). These are those very beings and the Lord of Beings, the year. He poured his seed into the Dawn;
in the course of a year, a boy was born. He wept. (6.1.3)
Prajāpati said to him:

"O boy, why do you weep, since you have been born from the toil of austerity? He replied: "I am indeed one whose evil has not been struck down and who has no assigned name; give me a name. Therefore, for a son who has been born—
He should give him a name; thereby he drives away his evil. Even a second time, even a third time, he thus drives away his evil in succession. 6.1.3. [10] He said to him, "You are Rudra."

Now, that name which he gave it became its form; Agni is Rudra because he wept (rud), and therefore he is called Rudra. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me another name. He said to him, "Thou art Sarva."

Now, when he gave it that name, water became its form; for indeed, everything is water, since from water all this is born. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me a name as well. He said to him, "You are Paśupati (Lord of Beasts)."
Now, that which he made his name became the form of the plants; for Paśupati is indeed the plants.
Therefore, when cattle obtain plants, they become masters (patīyanti). He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give to me [another]."
"Name," [he said].
He said to him, "You are Ugra (the Fierce). Because he gave him that name, Vāyu became his form; for Vāyu is indeed fierce.
Therefore, when there is a powerful wind, they say, "A fierce wind blows. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me a name as well.
They said to him, "You are Aśani (the Thunderbolt)."
Now, whatever name he gave it, that became its form: lightning. Indeed, lightning is a thunderbolt;
therefore, when lightning strikes someone, they say, "The thunderbolt has killed him. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me a name as well. 6.1.3 [15]
Bhava said to him, "Thou art Bhava.
Now, because he gave him that name, Parjanya became his form;
for Parjanya is indeed Bhava, since from Parjanya all this comes into being. He said, "I am indeed greater than that; grant me [a name] as well."
"Name," [he said]. 6.1.3.[16] To him the Great God said, "Thou art Asī.
Now, as for that which belongs to him...
He gave it the name "Candramas," and it became that form. Prajāpati indeed is Candramas;
Prajāpati is the Great God. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me a name as well.
He said to him, "You are Īśāna."
Now, that name which he gave to him, Āditya became his form.
Indeed, Īśāna is Āditya, for Āditya rules over all this. He said, "I am indeed as much as this; do not give me a name greater than this. These are those eight forms of Agni.
The boy is the ninth; he himself is Agni as the threefold [Gāyatrī].
Or rather, there are eight forms of Agni, and the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; therefore they say, "Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. This is he.
The youth entered into these forms; people do not see the youth as such, but they see these very forms of his, for he entered into these forms.
One should pile this [altar] during the year itself.

"One should recite [the invitatory verse] after a year," so some say; "for they shed that seed after a year, and after a year the boy was born; therefore one should pile [the altar] after two years and recite after two years. But rather, one should pile it after a year and recite after a year; for such indeed is the nature of seed.

That very [substance] which has been sprinkled is born; being modified from that state, it lies there increasing. Therefore, one should pile [the fire-altar] in a year and recite the formulas in a year. He gives a name to that which has been piled; thereby he strikes away its evil.
He gives it a bright name, saying, "Thou art bright (citra)," for Agni is indeed all that is bright. 6.2.1.1.
Prajāpati meditated upon the forms. He sought after that boy who had entered into the forms; he found him, and Agni thought: "Truly, my father Prajāpati seeks me; well then, let me become that form."
"Since he did not know this," [it is said]. He saw these five sacrificial animals:
the man, the horse, the cow, the sheep, and the goat; because he saw them, therefore they [are called *paśus*].
[The animals] 6.2.1.[3].
He entered these five animals; he became these five animals. Prajāpati indeed searched for him. 6.2.1.[4]
He saw these five animals; because he saw them, they are called "animals" (paśu); and because he saw this [Self] within them, they are indeed called "animals. 6.2.1[5]

He reflected: "These indeed are fires; I shall construct myself out of these very things. Just as fire, when kindled, blazes forth, so does their eye blaze forth; just as smoke rises from fire, so does their heat rise;
just as fire burns what is placed upon it, so do they eat; just as the ashes of fire settle down, so does theirs."
"The excrement sinks; these [fires] are indeed Agni; let me fashion them for myself. Thinking thus, he intended to offer them to various deities:
a man to Viśvakarman, a horse to Varuṇa, a bull to Indra, a ram to Tvaṣṭṛ, and a goat to Agni. 6.2.1. [6]

He reflected: "I have indeed intended these for various deities; I desire the forms of Agni; come, let me offer them to the Agnis for the sake of my desire. He offered them to the Agnis for the sake of his desire.
Now, as to why it is said "to the Agnis," it is because he meditated upon many forms of Agni; and as to why it is said "for the sake of desire," it is because he offered them out of desire.
Having led those [animals], which had been encircled by fire and were not yet prepared for sacrifice, toward the north, he caused them to be immolated.
He reflected: "The prosperity that I have bestowed, all that is now in their heads; come, let me place the heads themselves [as bricks].
So, having cut off the heads, he placed them down, and as for the other trunks, he cast them into the waters. With a goat, he [completed] the sacrifice.

"May my sacrifice not be torn asunder"—the sacrifice is indeed the self; [he thinks], "May this self of mine not be torn asunder. Having sacrificed with this animal, Prajāpati saw that he could not reach the end of this fire.
He reflected: "I must seek out that self of mine which floated away into the waters."

He searched for it; he found that which had remained firm when these [waters] were poured out into the waters. He gathered those waters together, and that clay which was upon this earth—having brought both together, the clay and the waters, he made them into bricks. Therefore, a brick consists of both of these: clay and water. 6.2.1. [9]

He reflected: "If I were to prepare this very being as food for myself," he cooked it with fire; that made it immortal. This is indeed the sacrificial oblation (havis) that is immortal. [Thinking,] "I shall become a mortal corpse, not freed from evil," he said, "Come now, let this which they cook with fire become cooked by fire."

Therefore, they bake the bricks with fire; verily, they thereby make them immortal. Now, because he saw [them] after sacrificing with an animal, therefore they are called *iṣṭakā*; thus, one should indeed sacrifice with an animal before making the bricks.

Those [acts] which they perform before the animal sacrifice would bring about what is undesirable; moreover, that [subsequent act] is indeed something quite different. 6.2.1. Those which were those splendors (*śrī*) are these heads of the animals; and those which were those trunks (*kusindha*) are these five [toes].
The layers are those; for having placed the heads of the animals, he builds the layers. By means of these very heads, he thus joins together these trunks.
All these animals are indeed the fire-altar.

Therefore, animals delight in the fire; in this [fire] the fire is established, for these animals are indeed the fire. Thus, by means of the breaths, the animals delight in that [fire] of Prajāpati. Therefore, for whomsoever...
They become cattle; by means of them Agni came into being. With all these, Prajāpati was about to sacrifice here.
That indeed is the limit of Agni.
Regarding this, some say:

"One should sacrifice with all these animals right here; for if one were to sacrifice with all these here, one would go to the very end of Agni. One should not do so, for he would then overstep the gods and stray from the path. Furthermore, what would he gather from there? For he gathers these very "channels" (kusindhas) as these layers (citīs).
Therefore, one should not do it in that way. Furthermore, as to why he immolates these animals: he thereby provides a dwelling-place for Agni, for no one indeed remains without a dwelling-place.
Food indeed delights in its abode; he places this [food] down in front, and Agni, beholding it, turns toward him.
A man, a horse, a cow, a sheep, and a goat are used;
for all animals are as many as these, and they are food.
Animals are food; he places this in front, and Agni, beholding it, turns toward him.
There are five [bricks], for these five layers are these fires; he thus provides these five abodes for them.
Then, seeing him, Agni turns back toward him.
As for the words "to the fires":
these altars are indeed many fires; and as for the words "for whatever desire": it is just as he [intends].
The sacrificer shall obtain whatever desire he performs this rite with.
He first seizes a human;
for the human is the first of animals; then a horse, then a human.

The horse follows the horse, the cow follows the horse, the sheep follows the cow, and the goat follows the sheep; thus he immolates them in their proper order, according to their excellence. Their ropes should be of unequal lengths.

The ropes for the animals are made according to the size of the man—some longest, some shorter, and some shortest—to avoid confusion; however, they should all indeed be equal, all similar, for all these fires are equal and all are similar, since they are called "food. Therefore, they should be equal and similar.

[The bricks] are equal by virtue of being similar. 6.2.1.[20] Regarding this, they say: "How does this fire of his, consisting of five bricks, become entirely undertaken in the sacrificial animals? [The answer is: "It is indeed obtained in the potsherds for the sacrificial cakes; this is the first brick made of clay. Then, when he immolates the animal..."
By that, the animal-brick is obtained; then, in that there are two pieces of gold on both sides of the omentum, by that the gold-brick is obtained;

then, in that there are the fuel-wood, the sacrificial post, and the enclosing-sticks, by that the wood-brick is obtained; then, in that there are the clarified butter, the sprinkling-waters, and the cake, by that the food-brick, the fifth, is obtained. Thus indeed does this [altar] of his come to be.
The entire fire-altar consists of five bricks and is commenced with the animal sacrifice.
For these, there are twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses;
for the year indeed consists of twenty-four half-months, and the year is [the altar].
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he thus kindles him. And again, as to why there are twenty-four:
the Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables; [Agni] is of the nature of the Gāyatrī."
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he thus kindles him. And as to why there are twenty-four [verses]:
man is indeed twenty-fourfold—ten fingers of the hands, ten [fingers of the feet],"
The foot has four syllables; Puruṣa is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus kindles him. He recites both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *gāyatrī*, and the self (*ātman*) is the *triṣṭubh*. By means of the *gāyatrīs* he kindles his vital breath, and by means of the *triṣṭubhs* he kindles his self. The *triṣṭubhs* are in the middle and the *gāyatrīs* are on both sides; for this self is in the middle, and the vital breaths are on both sides. He recites more *gāyatrīs* in front.
"The vital breaths here below are more numerous, for these vital breaths are indeed more numerous in the lower part and fewer in the upper part.
6.2.1 [25] He recites: "O Agni, may the years and the seasons strengthen thee. When Agni restored the relaxed Prajāpati, he said to him:
"With those kindling verses (*sāmidhenī*) that are commensurate with me, with those do thou enkindle me. 6.2.1 [26]
He saw these [verses]:
"O Agni, may the seasons and the years increase thee"—that is to say, "may both the seasons and the years increase thee";
"the years, the seers, and the truths"—that is to say, "the years, the seers, and the truths."

"May they increase [thee]"—this [is the meaning]. "Shine forth with the divine radiance"—the sun, indeed, is the divine radiance; thus, "shine forth with that," is what it means. "Illumine all four quarters"—that is, "illumine all four directions. These [verses] have a single explanation. 6.2.1 [27]
It is for this very purpose that one should prepare him, join him together, and generate him.
They belong to Agni and to Prajāpati: because Agni saw them, they belong to Agni; because he kindled them with Prajāpati, they belong to Prajāpati. 6.2.1 [28]
There are twelve Āprī verses.
There are twelve months in a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus gratifies him. 6.2.1.[29]
Or again, why twelve?
The Jagatī indeed consists of twelve syllables; this earth is the Jagatī, for upon it all this world moves.
Moreover, this earth is Agni, for upon it the entire Agni is built up. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—so much is it.
By that much indeed he gratifies him.
And as to why there are twelve:
the Jagatī consists of twelve syllables; the Jagatī is all the metres; all the metres [are thus represented].

"Prajāpati is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus gratifies him. "These are his upward-pointing fuel-sticks," [it is said]. When Prajāpati had become relaxed, there [Agni appeared]...
He composed himself and said to him, "With those *āprī* verses that correspond to me, do thou gratify me.
He beheld these [verses]:
"His fuel-sticks rise upward," for indeed, the fuel-sticks of this [fire] when kindled rise upward.

"The fuel-sticks of Agni are upright, his bright flames rising high"—for indeed, his bright flames and rays are upright; "most radiant"—that is, most powerful; "of the fair-faced one"—for Agni is fair-faced on all sides; "of the son"—because he generates him, therefore he is his son. 6.2.1 [33]

These [verses] have a single explanation. They refer to this very [sacrificial person]; just as one would prepare him, join him together, and generate him, so they are addressed to Agni and to Prajāpati: because Agni saw them, they are addressed to Agni; because he gratified Prajāpati with them, they are addressed to Prajāpati.
The *prājāpatya* verses (6.2.1) [34]:
they are uneven, having an uneven number of feet; they have an uneven number of syllables, for the meters (*candāṃsi*) are indeed uneven. Furthermore...
With these [verses], he gratifies those members of his own body that are uneven.
The sacrificial cake for the animal sacrifice is dedicated to Vaiśvānara;
for all fires are indeed Vaiśvānara, and it is for the attainment of all the fires.
Moreover, as for Vaiśvānara:

these layers (citayas) are indeed the seasons, or rather, the fires are the seasons; the seasons are the year, and Vaiśvānara is the year. If one were to say "the fires," that would be redundant; [therefore] it is on twelve potsherds, for there are twelve months.

The year; Vaiśvānara is indeed the year. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses belong to Agni, for the attainment of the forms of Agni. They contain the word "desire" (*kāma*), for the attainment of desires. 6.2.1.
[37] Now, some, having identified these as the heads of animals, place them down, thinking, "By both means these are animals. But they...
"Men become corpses, for those [bones] are indeed lifeless.
Now, they once placed these [bones] for Āṣāḍha Sauśromateya; he died very quickly thereafter.
Some, however, make them out of gold.
Saying, "They are bricks of immortality," they call them so; yet they are indeed bricks of falsehood, for those heads of animals are not made of clay.
However, some people do make them out of clay.
"These animals have indeed perished; for whatever has perished, this earth is the support of it all. Therefore, we shall collect them from wherever these animals have gone. One should not do so.
For those who do not know the ritual procedure (*āvṛt*) and the Brāhmaṇa explanation regarding these [animals], their animals would truly be lost. He...

One should sacrifice these very five animals as many times as one has the means. Prajāpati was the first to sacrifice them; Śyāparṇa Sāyakāyana was the last. Now, they used to sacrifice these same ones in between. But nowadays, only these two are sacrificed: the one dedicated to Prajāpati and the one dedicated to Vāyu. Regarding these two, the Brāhmaṇa is recited hereafter. 6.2.2. [1]
The Carakas sacrifice an animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Having piled the fire-altar, Prajāpati became Agni; therefore, when he sacrifices this animal, he reaches the very end of Agni. 6.2.2. [2]
He becomes dark-colored (*śyāma*).

Indeed, the hair of one who is dark-colored is of two kinds: white and black; this is a pair, a productive couple, and that is his form belonging to Prajāpati. He becomes hornless (*tūpara*), for Prajāpati is indeed hornless. 6.2.2. [3]
Its *sāmidhenī* verses are twenty-one.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first; this is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—
By that much he thus kindles him. And as to why there are twenty-one: man indeed consists of twenty-one parts—ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and [the body itself].
The Puruṣa Prajāpati consists of twenty-one parts; Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus kindles him. He recites both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs.
The connection of these verses has been stated; indeed, the *anuvāka* has been explained.

He pours the *āghāra* libation with a verse containing the word "Hiraṇyagarbha. Hiraṇyagarbha is Prajāpati, and Agni is Prajāpati. There are twelve *Āprī* verses; their connection has been stated, and indeed the *anuvāka* has been explained as belonging to Prajāpati.

The sacrificial cake for the animal sacrifice has the same significance as that of the animal itself. It is prepared on twelve potsherds; there are twelve months in a year, and the year is Prajāpati. The invitatory and offering verses contain the word *ka*, for Prajāpati is indeed *Ka*. Then [he offers] this [cake] to Vāyu Niyutvat.
One sacrifices a white, hornless goat. Prajāpati, having created the creatures, gazed upon them; through excessive joy, his seed fell away, and it became this white, hornless goat with testicles.
Seed is indeed essence (*rasa*); as great as the essence is, so great is the self (*ātman*). Therefore, when one sacrifices this [animal].

He thus goes around the very end of Agni; it is white, for semen is white; it is hornless, for semen is hornless; it is for Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*); it is for Niyutvat; Niyuts are indeed the up-breath (*udāna*); he thus bestows both the out-breath and the up-breath upon him. 6.2.2. [7]
Furthermore, as for why he offers this white, hornless goat to Vāyu Niyutvat: when the gods restored Prajāpati after he had fallen apart,
that vital breath which had departed from his center— by means of this [offering], they placed it back into him.

They offered it with a domestic animal; in the same way, he now offers this for him. It is for Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*). It is for Niyutvat; Niyuts are indeed the up-breath (*udāna*). Thus, he places both the out-breath and the up-breath in him. It is white, for Vāyu is white;
it is hornless (*tūpara*), for Vāyu is hornless. 6.2.2. [8]
For this sacrifice, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
The year is indeed seventeenfold: twelve months and five seasons;
the year is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—so much is it.
By this much he kindles him. And as to why there are seventeen: man indeed consists of seventeen parts—there are ten vital breaths, four limbs, and the self is the fifteenth.

The necks are the sixteenfold [stomas], the head is the seventeenfold; Prajāpati is the Puruṣa, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much does he thus kindle him. He recites both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs.
The *bandhu* of these has been stated; indeed, the *anuvāka* following the verse has been stated.
There are twelve *apriya* verses; their *bandhu* has been stated; indeed, the *anuvāka* following the verse has been stated. The animal-cake offering belongs to Prajāpati;
"In this, that desire is attained," so said Māhitthi, regarding what the Carakas say concerning the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati. 6.2.2. [11]

Furthermore, as to why there is an animal sacrifice for Vāyu and a sacrificial cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for Prajāpati: Vāyu is one half of Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the other half. Therefore, if both were for Vāyu, or if both were for Prajāpati—

Indeed, half of him would have been prepared for Prajāpati, but not the other half; however, because there is an animal sacrifice for Vāyu and an animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for Prajāpati, by that very means he prepares this entire, complete Prajāpati. Furthermore, as to why there is an animal sacrifice for Vāyu...

The animal-cake belongs to Prajāpati. When the gods restored Prajāpati after he had become disjointed, they placed that vital breath which had departed from his center back into him by means of this animal;
then they restored his body by means of this cake. That it belongs to Prajāpati is for this reason.
For Prajāpati is the self; the cake on twelve potsherds has twelve parts, and the year consists of twelve months; Prajāpati is the year.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word "ka," for Prajāpati is "Ka. Now, as to why he offers the omentum first:
Whatever this vital breath (prāṇa) is that is in front, it is that he places in him by this [offering].

And when they proceed with this in the middle, it is because this self (ātman) is in the middle. And when they proceed with the oblation from above, it is that vital breath which is above; he places that in him by this. The invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā) should contain the word "white" (śukla).
For the attainment of white forms, there are [verses] containing the word *niyut*; this is for the attainment of that form which possesses *niyuts*.
Regarding this, they say:
"The two [verses] should belong to the omentum (*vapā*) itself; for this much indeed is the white in the animal."
"Because there are two omenta, one with white spots and one with many spots; it is for the attainment of that form of his which consists of the *niyut* [team].
6.2.2.[15] And as to why he immolates this animal:
in this animal, indeed, is the form of all animals, namely, that it is hornless (*tūpara*).
The *lapsudī* is the form of the *tatpuruṣa* compound; for a man who is barren is a *lapsudī*.

That he has a mane is the form of the horse, for a horse that has a mane is a *tūpara*. That he has eight hooves is the form of the cow, for a cow has eight hooves. Now, in that his hooves are like those of a sheep, that is the form of the sheep; and in that he is a goat, that is the form of the goat.
In that he sacrifices this [animal], by that very act all these animals of his become sacrificed.
Therefore, whichever of these rites may be prepared for him— whether it be these five animals, or this one dedicated to Prajāpati, or this one dedicated to Niyutvat—
he should sacrifice it on the full moon day.

"One should sacrifice on the new moon day," so some say; "for that moon is Prajāpati, and he dwells here on this night; thus it is as if one were to sacrifice to him while he is present. But [the correct view is] that it should indeed be on the full moon day.
That moon is indeed the sacrificial animal; the gods offer it at the full moon.
Thinking, "Where the gods offer this, there let us also offer it," they therefore offer it at the full moon. Furthermore, as to why it is at the full moon:
the full moon was indeed the first night that dawned; for that reason also, they offer it at the full moon. 6.2.2 [18]

That indeed takes place on the Phālgunī day itself. For this Phālgunī full moon is the first night of the year; that which is the later [Phālgunī] is the last. Thus, by means of the former, one begins the year at its very beginning. 6.2.2.[19]

Having indeed performed the full-moon sacrifice, he should then immolate the animal victim; for by performing the full-moon sacrifice, Indra, having slain Vṛtra—the evil—and being freed from evil, undertook this rite. In the same way, the sacrificer does so now.
Having slain Vṛtra, who is evil, by means of the Full-moon sacrifice itself, he, with evil removed, undertakes this rite.
That [sacrifice] indeed takes place in a whisper;
for it was by means of these animals that Prajāpati sought to perform this rite.
Therefore, it is as if woven by the Creator, as if unexpressed; for that reason, [the recitation is] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
And furthermore, as to why it is in a low voice:
this ritual action belongs to Prajāpati, for one undertakes this ritual action with reference to Prajāpati, who is himself unexpressed.

Verily, Prajāpati [is the deity]. 6.2.2.[22] And as to why it is in a low voice (*upāṃśu*): seed indeed is here in the sacrifice; and in a low voice, seed is emitted—the omentum (*vapā*) and the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
"For the oblation is only this much, for the animal sacrifice is only this much.
On the Aṣṭakā day, he collects the fire-pan (ukhā);
for this day belonging to the Aṣṭakā belongs to Prajāpati, and this rite belongs to Prajāpati.
In that he prepares the fire-pan on the day sacred to Prajāpati, he performs a rite dedicated to Prajāpati.
Furthermore, as for [its preparation] on the Aṣṭakā:
the Aṣṭakā is a festival of the year, and the fire-pan is a festival of Agni.
On the very day of the *parvan*, he performs that *parvan* rite.
Or rather, it is on the *aṣṭakā*.
For the *ukhā* is indeed the *aṣṭakā*; the two supports are the bottom and the top, and the girdle is the crosswise line; thus it consists of four layers.
He makes those eight [verses] of the eightfold [hymn] into an eightfold [hymn] by means of the eightfold [hymn] itself.
6.2.2.[26] He undergoes initiation on the new moon day;
for it is from the new moon that the sacrifice is extended. From where the sacrifice is extended, from there he extends the sacrifice.
"May I bring forth," [he thinks].
Furthermore, when it is on the new moon day (amāvāsyā),
he who undergoes consecration (dīkṣate) pours his own self, which has become semen, into the fire-pan (ukhā) as a womb.
Therefore, he creates this world beforehand when he undergoes initiation; he is born toward that world once it has been created.
Hence they say: "A person is born toward a world already made. 6.2.2.
[28] Now, if he were to be initiated for less than a year...

If he were to lay down the bricks first and then the worlds, the worlds would exceed the bricks; and if, having made many worlds, he were not to lay down the bricks accordingly, the bricks would exceed the worlds. Now, when he undergoes initiation on the new-moon day and purchases [the Soma] on the new-moon day, then as much space as there is—
He performs [the rites] for as many [days] as there are bricks he lays down; then, during the waxing fortnight, his entire fire-altar is built.

Regarding this, they say: "If the days and nights of the purchase [of Soma] amount to as many as the bricks of this fire-altar, then what of those days after the purchase—how are those worlds of his laid down? Or rather...

Having been initiated on the new moon day, he purchases [the Soma] on the new moon day. Thus, as large a world as he makes, so many bricks does he lay down. Now, during those days following the purchase, the Adhvaryu builds the fire-altar in that interval; for where else could he build it, since there would be no other space? Indeed, as many as are the days and nights of the year, so many [are those days].

The bricks of this fire-altar are also thirteen, for the thirteenth month is indeed that which consists of the days following the purchase [of the Soma]. Those bricks which belong to the thirteenth month—with them these worlds of his become laid down; thus the worlds and the bricks become equal. 6.2.2. [30]

On that very first full moon, he immolates the animal victim; on that which is the first Aṣṭakā, he collects the materials for the fire-pan (ukhā); on that which is the first new moon, he undergoes initiation (dīkṣā). Indeed, these are...
The first days of the year—those he begins with this [rite], and those he thereby attains.
Now, therefore, regarding the correspondence [of the rite]: they say, "How does this ritual act of his attain Agni the Year? How [does it correspond] with Agni the Year?"
Thus, for these five animals, there are twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses, twelve *āprī* verses, eleven *anuyāja* offerings, and eleven *upayāja* offerings; that makes fifty-eight.
From that, forty-eight remain.

This *jagatī* consists of forty-eight syllables. Indeed, this is the *jagatī*, for upon it all this world moves. Moreover, this is Agni, for upon her the entire Agni is piled up. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become. 6.2.2. [33]
Or again, as to why there are forty-eight:
the Jagatī consists of forty-eight syllables; the Jagatī is all the meters;
all the meters are Prajāpati; Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become. 6.2.2.[34]
Now, those which are ten—that is the Virāj of ten syllables; Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths.
As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become. 6.2.2 [35]
The omentum and the animal cake—these make sixty;
there are sixty days and nights in a month. He thus attains the month; the month attained, he attains the season; the season, the year.
Thus he attains the year and the fires, as well as the desires that are contained within the year. And then...
Whatever other food there is in the year, that is all [the food].
Now, for this sacrifice to Prajāpati, there are twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses.

There are twelve fore-offerings; thirty-three are the *anuyāja*s, eleven the *upayaj*s—this makes fifty-five. There is the omentum, the animal cake, and the oblation—this makes fifty-eight. Whatever desire there is in fifty-eight, that he obtains right here.
There are two *āghāra* libations—this makes sixty. Whatever desire there is in sixty, that he obtains right here. Now, as for what follows this...
Whatever food there is in the year, that is all this [sacrifice].
Now, regarding this Niyutvatīya [offering]:
there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses and twelve *āprī* verses; thus, one [verse] is not [recited].
There are thirty-one after-offerings (*anuyāja*s) and eleven by-offerings (*upayāja*s), which makes fifty-one; the omentum, the animal cake, and the oblation make fifty-four;

the two libations (*āghāra*) and the two *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings make fifty-eight. Whatever desire there is regarding the number fifty-eight, one attains it right here. Furthermore, the offering to the Lord of the Forest (*vanaspati*) and the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*) make sixty. Whatever [desire there is regarding that]...

On the sixth [day], Kāma [is the deity]; he attains him right here. Now, whatever other food there is besides this—whatever food exists in the year—all that very food he thus attains through this rite; in this way, he becomes united with Agni through the year. 6.2.2. [38]

Regarding this they say: "One should not offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations for this animal sacrifice, nor should one descend into the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the heart-spit. For this animal is the commencement of the fire-ritual, while the *samiṣṭayajus* are the relinquishment of the deities and the *avabhṛtha* is the conclusion. [Thus,] let me not relinquish the deities at the very commencement, nor the sacrifice."

Thinking, "I shall conclude it," he should indeed conclude it; having sacrificed with this animal, Prajāpati saw that he did not reach the end of this fire-altar. Therefore, one should conclude it. And furthermore, as to why he concludes it:
this animal is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); whatever were to be omitted from it, that would be omitted from the vital breath. Whatever...

If he were to let the breath depart from him, he would die in that very way; therefore, one should keep it steady. Now, concerning the vows: they say, "Having sacrificed with this animal, one should not sleep on a raised bed, nor eat meat, nor engage in sexual intercourse. For this animal is the preliminary consecration (*dīkṣā*); it is improper for one who is consecrated to sleep on a raised bed."

"One should sleep, eat meat, and engage in sexual intercourse"—this is not truly a consecration (dīkṣā), for there is no girdle here, nor a black antelope skin. Rather, he makes this very [act] his brick; therefore, one may indeed sleep at will on top.
All this food which these animals eat is obtained and undertaken by him here; thus, whatever [things] there are...

Among all those foods, including curds and honey, if one were to obtain the eating of all these desires, yet he should not approach a woman before the *maitrāvaruṇī* curd-mixture; the significance of this is explained later.
Regarding this, they say: "One should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at this sacrifice, lest this sacrifice of mine be without a fee, O Brahman."
"One should give the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); for the Brahman is indeed the whole sacrifice, and thus his entire sacrifice becomes successful.

One should not do so; for he thereby makes this [Brahman] a brick. Just as one would give [the fee] for each individual brick, so it would be in that case. Therefore, he should give it on that very day whatever may be available to him. 6.2.3. [1]

The gods indeed said this: "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek ye a layer. While they were reflecting, Prajāpati beheld this first naturally perforated layer; therefore, that [layer is so called].

He lays it down with the Prajāpati [formula]. 6.2.3.[2] Agni said to him: "I shall come to you. "By what means? "By means of cattle. "So be it. Thus, by means of the animal-brick (paśviṣṭakā), he indeed...

Regarding this, he said: "This, indeed, is the animal-brick, namely the *dūrvā*-brick. Therefore, the *dūrvā*-brick is placed immediately adjacent to the first naturally-perforated (*svayamātṛṇā*) brick. Hence, plants are not separated from it; animals are not separated from it; and Agni is not separated from it—for he is approached by means of this very brick. 6.2.3. [3]
They said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)!"—"Seek it from here upwards!
As they were thus reflecting, Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman perceived the atmosphere as the second naturally-perforated layer; therefore, he places that [layer] with Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman.
Vāyu said to them, "I shall come to you.
He asked, "By what means? They replied, "By the quarters (diś). He said, "So be it. Thus he spoke by means of the *diśyā* bricks;
therefore, the *diśyā* bricks are laid down immediately adjacent to the second naturally perforated (*svayamātṛṇā*) brick.
Therefore, from that intermediate space, the quarters are not separated; the wind is not separated; for he approached these [worlds] by means of those which were not separated.
They said, "Meditate indeed!"—by this they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)," or rather, "Seek upward from here.
While they were meditating, Parameṣṭhin saw the sky as the third self-perforated layer (svayamātṛṇā citi); therefore, that [layer] belongs to him.
He lays it down with the *parameṣṭhi* [formula]. 6.2.3.[6] Tamaḥ said to that Āditya: "I shall come to you. "By what means? "By the *lokampṛṇā* [brick]. "So be it. This indeed is...

He spoke that very thing with the nature of the *lokampṛṇā*; therefore, the third *svayamātṛṇā* is placed immediately adjacent to the *lokampṛṇā*. Therefore, the sun is not separated from the sky, for it is indeed not separated from it by means of this [brick]. These, then, are the six deities.
"All this that exists here has become these [beings].

The gods and the seers said, "These six deities have indeed become all this; find out how we too may be present here. They said, "Seek a layer (cit). By this they meant, "Seek a way," for they were saying, "Seek that. Seek it!
"May we also be here," they thought. While they were thus reflecting, the gods perceived the second layer (*citi*), and the seers (*ṛṣis*) perceived the fourth.
They said, "Let us approach. [The others asked,] "By what means? [They replied,] "By that which approaches within these worlds. "So be it. Then, that which is above...
That which is on this side of the earth and on the other side of the atmosphere—by that the gods attained [the world]; that is this second layer.
Now, that which is above the atmosphere and below the sky—by that the seers attained [the world]; that is this fourth layer. 6.2.3.
[9] As for what they said:
"Reflect upon it! they said; by this they meant, "Seek the layer. Because they saw [the layers] while reflecting, they are called *citayas* (layers). Prajāpati perceived the first layer.
Prajāpati alone was its seerhood; the gods saw the second layer; the gods alone were its seerhood; Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman saw the third layer;
they alone were its seerhood; the Ṛṣis saw the fourth layer; the Ṛṣis alone were its [seerhood].

Parameṣṭhin saw the fifth layer as having Parameṣṭhin for its seer; Parameṣṭhin indeed is the seer-connection of that layer. He who thus knows the seer-connections of the layers, his layers become possessed of seers and possessed of kinship. 6.3.1. [1] This, indeed, the gods said.
"Reflect! he said; "Seek a layer (citiḥ)! was indeed what he meant to say.
While they were reflecting, Savitṛ saw these Sāvitra formulas. Because Savitṛ saw them, they are called Sāvitra.
He offered this eightfold-drawn oblation, and that—
Having offered this [oblation], he saw the Aṣāḍhā brick, which had been created long before and was now established in eight parts.

When they said, "Meditate! (*cetayadhvam*), they were indeed saying, "Seek a layer" (*citim icata*). Because they saw it while meditating, it is called a *citi*. The oblation is indeed the sacrifice; because he saw it after sacrificing, it is called an *iṣṭakā* (brick).
This very [offering], though being one, he offers with eight *yajuṣ* formulas consisting of eight portions; therefore, this [earth], though being one, is established in eight ways.
He offers it while holding it upwards.
He takes this [earth] upwards by means of forms; therefore, this [earth] is upwards by means of forms. He offers it as a continuous stream.

The gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* and destroyers (*nāṣṭrās*) should follow after us here. They saw this continuous oblation for the purpose of preventing the *rakṣases* and destroyers from following after them;
therefore, he offers it continuously. 6.3.1. [6]
Moreover, as to why he offers this oblation:

this Agni is Savitṛ; he gratifies him beforehand with this oblation. Having sacrificed to him and gratified him, he then gathers him together. Because he gratifies Savitṛ with this, they are called *sāvitrāṇi*; that is why they are so named.
He offers this oblation.
And as to why he offers this oblation:
this fire is Savitṛ; with this oblation he pours it forth in front as seed.
In whatever kind of womb the seed is poured, such [a being] is born; since he pours Savitṛ as the seed by means of this [verse], they are called *sāvitrāṇi*.
For this reason, he offers this oblation.
Here, both the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles are employed.

Speech is indeed the *sruk* ladle and breath is the *sruva* spoon; for by means of speech and breath, the gods first performed this ritual action. Therefore there is both the *sruva* and the *sruk*. Furthermore, as to why there is both the *sruva* and the *sruk*:

He who was Prajāpati is this very *sruva* spoon; the *sruva* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and Prajāpati is the vital breath. And she who was Speech is this very *sruc* ladle; Speech is indeed female, and the *sruc* is female. And those waters which went forth from the world of Speech—those are these [waters] for which he offers this oblation. 6.3.1. [10]
He offers that [oblation] continuously;

for those waters flowed continuously. Now, he who was Prajāpati entered the waters together with the threefold knowledge (trayi vidyā)—he is this very one by whom one offers these sacrificial formulas (yajus). 6.3.1. [11]

Those which are the first three are these worlds; then that which is the fourth *yajus* is the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), it is the *jagatī*; it becomes the *jagatī*, for all the meters are the *jagatī*, and all the meters are the triple knowledge. Then those which are the four last [verses]—

The quarters are indeed these worlds, and the quarters are Prajāpati; moreover, this is the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā). 6.3.1.[12] He offers [the oblation], saying: "He who yokes the first mind. Prajāpati is indeed the one who yokes; he yoked the mind for this rite.
Because he yoked the mind for this rite, therefore Prajāpati is "the one who yokes" (yuñjānaḥ). 6.3.1.[13]
"For Savitṛ, having perceived the light of Agni, has brought [the oblation] from the earth for the sake of truth and for the sake of thought.
Savitṛ is indeed the mind; thoughts are the vital breaths. "Having perceived the light of Agni" means "having seen the light of Agni"; "he has brought [it] from the earth" means "from the earth."
With the verse, "With a yoked mind, may we... (RV 10.20.9), he brings [the butter] from this [vessel].
He thereby yokes the mind itself for this ritual action; for with an unyoked [mind], it cannot be performed.

"By means of the mind, he is now able to perform something at the impulsion of the god Savitṛ. This means "impelled by the god Savitṛ. "With power for the sake of heaven"—he says this so that by this rite he may go to the heavenly world; "with power," he says, for it is by power that one goes to the heavenly world. 6.3.1 [15]

"Having yoked the gods, Savitṛ," for Savitṛ is indeed the mind and the gods are the vital breaths; "going to heaven with prayer to the sky," for he has yoked her with prayer for this rite to go to the heavenly world; "he will create the great light"—that [light] is yonder sun.

Or rather, the sun is the great light; he is indeed this Agni, whom they are about to consecrate. "Savitṛ shall impel them"—that is to say, "impelled by Savitṛ, may they perform this rite. (6.3.1) "They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts."

"The mind and these vital breaths he yokes for this rite"—the sage is Prajāpati, and the sages are the gods. "Of the great, wise one"—the great, wise one is indeed Prajāpati. "He ordains the priestly offices"—for when he is piled up, then he ordains the priestly offices for the one who has been piled.

For upon him these priestly offices (*hotrā*) are ordained; "the finder of the way" (*vayunāvit*), for he alone has found this way here; "the one alone," for he alone has found all this way; "great is the praise of the god Savitṛ"—that is to say, great is the praise of the god Savitṛ. 6.3.1 [17]
"I yoke for you both the ancient prayer with prostrations"—
the ancient prayer is indeed breath,
and the prostration is food; that is this very oblation, and it is by means of this oblation of food that he [reaches] "the presence of the patron," as in the case of both [classes].

Among gods and men, fame and renown [are gained]; by means of the sacrificial food, he yokes the vital breaths for this rite. "May the renown go forth like a path for us"—he says this so that it may be so. "May all the sons of immortality hear"—Prajāpati indeed is immortality, and all the gods are his sons. "Those who have taken their stand in the celestial abodes"—these worlds are indeed the celestial abodes.
"The abodes"—he thereby refers to those gods who are in these worlds. "Whose departure the others followed"—Prajāpati indeed performed this rite first; after that, the gods [followed].

"Performing by his might the greatness of the god"—the sacrifice is indeed the greatness; thus, "the gods [performed] the sacrifice, the heroism of the god, by his might. "He who has measured out the earthly realms, he is Etaśa"—whatever is on this earth is indeed the earthly;
all that he measures out, for with his rays he stretches across it, the god Savitṛ, over the regions.
"By greatness"—these worlds are indeed the *rajāṃsi*; that god Savitṛ, the Sun, measures them out by means of his greatness.
"O god Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for the sake of fortune.
That god is indeed the Sun.
"Savitṛ is the sacrifice, Bhaga; to him he says this: 'Impel the sacrifice, impel the lord of the sacrifice for the sake of Bhaga.
'May the divine Gandharva, the purifier of intentions (ketapūḥ), purify our intention'—for yonder Āditya is indeed the divine Gandharva, and intention is food;
thus, 'may he purify our food. 'May the Lord of Speech (Vācaspati) sweeten our speech'—for speech is indeed this ritual action."

"Prāṇa is the lord of speech; may Prāṇa make this rite of ours sweet"—this is what it means. "O God Savitṛ, lead this sacrifice of ours forward. Yonder sun is indeed the god Savitṛ; for he is that which is... [6.3.1.20]

He leads forward the sacrificial rite; he attains that which is uninjured, a successful conclusion, and prosperity. "Devāvya" means he who has praised the gods. "Sakhividam, satrājitam, dhanajitam, svarjitam" means he who would find all this.
"Rcā stomam samardhaya gāyatreṇa rathantaram" means: by means of the Ṛg-verse, fulfill the Stoma with the Gāyatra, [and] the Rathantara.

"The *bṛhat* and *gāyatra* paths" refers to the *sāmans*; "svāhā" refers to the *yajus* formulas. Thus, this threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) is born first, just as it was born there [in the beginning]; and that fire which was created then is this very fire which is built hereafter. These are the eight *sāvitra* verses.

The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just that much he pours him forth when he has become seed. These [syllables] become nine, the *svāhā*-utterance being the ninth;
there are nine quarters, and Agni is the quarters; there are nine vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure.
In this way, he pours out that seed once it has become such; these [oblations] become ten, with the tenth being the oblation itself.

The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become. 6.3.1. [22]

When this oblation had been offered, Agni went away from the gods. The gods said, "Agni is indeed an animal; let us search for him by means of animals; he will manifest himself in his own form. They searched for him with animals, and he—
It became manifest in its own form; therefore, indeed, an animal becomes manifest in its own form.

They said: "If we search with all [of us], they will become exhausted and unfit for subsistence—whether a cow for a cow, a horse for a horse, or a man for a man. But if we search with not all [of us], we shall find what is incomplete."
They saw this one animal as corresponding to two animals: the donkey, which belongs to both the cow and the sheep.
Because they saw this one animal as corresponding to two animals, therefore this [donkey], though being one, has double seed.
[They sought] the man who was not real from among men.

He indeed is the man who is not real who does not help the gods, nor the ancestors, nor men; therefore, they sought him with all their cattle, yet he did not become exhausted, nor was he available for them to subsist upon. 6.3.1 [25]
He seeks him with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus seeks him.
There are five in total: the fire-altar consists of five layers, there are five seasons in the year, and the year is the year.
"As great as fire is, as great as its measure is, so great does that become.
They are bound with cords made of muñja grass.
Fire departed from the gods; it entered the muñja grass.
Therefore, that cavity entered him; therefore, from within it, he is as if smoky-red.
This *muñja* grass is the womb of Agni. These cattle are Agni. Indeed, the womb does not harm the embryo; it is for the sake of non-injury.
For one who is being born is born from a womb; [he thinks], "May he be born from a womb. 6.3.1. [27]
They are threefold;

for Agni is threefold. They are made into horse-tethers; for the horse-tether encircles the mouth from all sides, and the womb encircles the embryo from all sides; thus this form of the womb is produced. 6.3.1.[28]
They stand facing east:
first the horse, then the donkey, then the goat; for these indeed follow one another in succession.
That which was the tear that flowed then is this horse; that which was the frothing [of the mouth] is this donkey; and that which was on the potsherd—
The juice was smeared; that was the goat. And that which was the skull-cup, that was this clay.
Intending to bring this [clay], they indeed produce him from these very forms, for from these forms he was created in the beginning.
They stand to the south.

The gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases*, the destroyers, should strike our sacrifice from the south. They saw this thunderbolt—namely, yonder sun; for yonder sun is this horse. Having struck away the *rakṣases*, the destroyers, from the south by means of this thunderbolt, they [performed] this [sacrifice] in a place free from danger and destruction.

In the same way, the sacrificer now extends this sacrifice; having struck away the Rakṣases and the destroyers from the south with this thunderbolt, he extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction.
The Āhavanīya fire is situated to the south.

This spade lies to the north; for the Āhavanīya fire is a male and the spade is a female, and the male indeed lies to the south of the female. It is at the distance of a cubit, for from the distance of a cubit the male lies beside the female. 6.3.1 [31]
That [sacrificial ladle] should be made of bamboo.
Agni departed from the gods; he entered the bamboo, which is why it is hollow. He created these joints on all sides as armor, for the purpose of not being recognized, wherever he was scorched.
They became spotted (kalmāṣa).
That [cow] should be spotted;
for she belongs to Agni. If one should not find a spotted one, it may even be non-spotted, provided it is hollow-horned.

It should be made of clay from a fire-pan; for that is the womb of Agni, and the bamboo is Agni, while this clay is the earth. Indeed, the womb does not harm the embryo; it is for the sake of non-injury. For one who is being born is born from a womb; [he thinks], "May he be born from a womb. It should be a span in length.
For speech speaks of this [post] as being only a span (prādeśa) long; however, it should indeed be a cubit (aratni) long.
The cubit is the arm, and by the arm valor is performed; thus, it becomes commensurate with valor.
It should be sharpened on one side. 6.3.1 [34]
For this speech is sharp on one side; it is, as it were, sharp on both sides, for this speech is indeed sharp on both sides:
because with it one speaks both what is divine and what is human, and also because it speaks both truth and untruth; therefore it is sharp on both sides. 6.3.1 [35]
And as to why it is sharp on both sides: from this very part of the flint comes its vigor; thus he bestows vigor upon her from both sides. 6.3.1 [36]
Furthermore, as to why it is sharpened on both sides:
the gods, having discovered him, dug him out from these worlds; in the same way, this [sacrificer], having discovered him, digs him out from these worlds. 6.3.1. [37]
When he digs thus, he digs him out from this world; then, when it rises upward, he digs him out from yonder world;
and when it moves between these two, he digs him out from the intermediate world—from all of them.

Thus he digs it out from these worlds. He takes it up with [the formula]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee. Impelled by Viśvakarman, he thus takes it up with these deities; with the Gāyatra [meter], with the hands of Pūṣan, he takes it up with the Gāyatra.

"With the *candas* of Aṅgiras"—thus, with the *candas*, he places the *gāyatrī* metre upon her. "From the seat of the earth, bring forth Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras"—for *purīṣa* is indeed cattle;
thus, "from the lap of the earth, bring forth Agni who is favorable to cattle in the manner of Agni. "With the *traiṣṭubha* metre in the manner of Aṅgiras"—thus [he says].
Thus he takes it up with the *triṣṭubh* metre; verily, he places the *triṣṭubh* metre within it.

"Thou art a spade," he says, for this [sacrificial post] is indeed a spade; thus he takes it up with truth. "Thou art a woman," he says; for the spade is a thunderbolt and a woman is a female; he does not [take it up] as a male.

A woman indeed harms no one; she merely pacifies her for the sake of non-injury. "With thee may we be able to dig out Agni in this common abode"—this common abode is indeed this [spot]; "with thee may we be able to dig out Agni in this common abode," he thereby says. "In the Jāgata metre, like Aṅgiras"—he thus [addresses her] with the Jāgata metre.
He takes it up with the Gāyatrī metre; then he places the Jāgata metre upon it.
He takes it up with three [verses];
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he thus takes it up.

Having taken it up with three [verses], he then consecrates it with the fourth; for the gods, having taken her up with three, then bestowed vigor upon her with the fourth. In the same way, this [sacrificer], having taken her up with three, bestows vigor upon her with the fourth. 6.3.1. [41]
"Having placed [it] in his hand, Savitṛ..."—for it is indeed placed in his hand; "bearing the unbaked [brick]..."—for he indeed bears it;
"the golden one..."—for this [brick] which is here is indeed made of gold.
"Having perceived the light of Agni Chandoma"—that is to say, "having seen the light of Agni"; "he brought it from the earth," for he indeed brings it from the earth;
"with the Anuṣṭubh metre, like Aṅgiras"—thereby he takes it up with the Anuṣṭubh metre, and thus he places the Anuṣṭubh metre in this [earth].
These very same *candāṃsi* (metres) are these; this bamboo *abhri* (spade) is made for the sake of undertaking [the sacrifice].
Some indeed make it golden, thinking, "It is described as being made of gold," but one should not do so; for as to what this [spade] is—
The *candāṃsi* (metres) are gold; gold is the immortal, and the *candāṃsi* are the immortals. 6.3.1 [43] He takes it up with four [verses].
For all speech consists of four syllables: "vāk" is one syllable, "akṣara" is [another] syllable...

That which consists of three syllables is "vāk" (speech); this is one syllable, which is that same *anuṣṭubh* which is the highest. And as for the word "akṣara," it consists of three syllables; these are those same former *yajus*-formulas. Thus, with the whole of speech he digs the fire-altar, and with the whole of speech he prepares it. Therefore, [he does so] with four [verses]. 6.3.1. [44]
Or rather, as to why he uses four:

there are indeed four quarters; he thus places speech in the four quarters, and therefore speech speaks in the four quarters. He takes it up with both *chandases* and *yajus* formulas; that makes eight—four quarters and four [quarters].
He places the speech in all the intermediate directions; therefore, speech speaks in all directions. 6.3.2.
[1] The spade is in his hand; then he consecrates the animals with a mantra.
For it was here that the gods, seeking them, found them.
In the beginning, they bestowed vigor upon them; likewise, he, seeking to find this [vigor] within them, bestows vigor upon them from the front.
He addresses the horse:
"O steed, run forth swiftly! For that which is rapid is indeed "tūrtam" (swift). And then...
"That which is swift, swifter than swift, the rushing, following the most excellent *saṃvat*": this earth, indeed, is the most excellent *saṃvat*;

"following this *saṃvat*" means this very thing. "In heaven is thy highest birth, in the atmosphere thy navel, upon the earth thy womb"—thereby he makes him these deities: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya; that [he does] in the horse.
He bestows vigor. 6.3.2.[3] Then [regarding] the donkey:
"Yoke the donkey, you two"—[with these words] he addresses both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
And in this watch, in this ritual act [beginning with] "O you two who possess rain-giving wealth," he places that [power] in the donkey;
[specifically], in the phrase "bearing Agni, well-disposed toward us," he places the sense of "bearing Agni, sent forth by us. 6.3.2. [4]
Then [he offers] the goat with the verse: "In every endeavor, we call upon the most powerful one; in every contest for booty... Food, indeed, is "booty" (*vāja*).

"In every action, we call upon the most powerful one in food after food"—this is what he says. "O friends, Indra for our protection... means "the possessor of power for our protection. Thus, he bestows vigor upon the goat. 6.3.2. [5]
He consecrates them with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows vigor upon these [bricks]. 6.3.2.[6]
Then he makes them step forward toward the east.
Thus he seeks him with these animals; he does not touch them, thinking, "Lest this fire, which is these animals, should injure me. 6.3.2. [7]
He makes the horse step forward with the formula:
"Speeding on, come hither; treading down the malevolent. Malevolence, indeed, is evil;
thus it means, "Come hither in haste, treading down evil. With the words, "The troop of Rudra, the source of bliss, come hither," for they belong to Rudra.
"O beast, come to that deity of yours, to the state of being Ganapati, bringing bliss"—this he says as he seeks him out with the horse.
6.3.2 [8] Then [he seeks out] the donkey:
"Traverse the wide atmosphere, creating security, good pastures, and fearlessness"—just as before.
The *yajus* formula, "With Pūṣan as his companion," means "with this [earth] as his companion. Thus, he seeks him out by means of the donkey.
