Then [he seeks] the goat: "From the seat of the earth, bring Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras"—[that is,] from the earth.
"Standing near, bring the Agni who is beneficial to cattle, like Agni himself"—this is how he searches for him with a goat.
He searches with three verses;
Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus searches for him.

He consecrates them with three [verses] from the front; that makes six. There are six seasons, and the year is the six seasons; Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does this become. These fires are set ablaze.
Now, as he gathers the clay—these fires are indeed these worlds;

when they are kindled, then these worlds are manifest. For it was before these worlds that the gods first performed their work. Therefore, when he brings the clay after passing over these fires, he thereby brings it from before these worlds.
He searches for him from the front. They go toward the east;
for the eastern quarter belongs to Agni. Thus he searches for him in his own quarter; in his own quarter he finds him.
They proceed:
"We would kindle Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras"—that is to say, "we would kindle the animal-loving Agni in the manner of Agni. 6.3.3.[4]

Then he looks at the Anaddhāpuruṣa: "We shall bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras"—that is to say, "we shall bear the fire-favoring Agni like Agni. Thus he seeks him out by means of the Anaddhāpuruṣa. 6.3.3 [5]
Now, an ant-hill with a hollow cavity is placed midway;
he gazes upon it, thinking:
"This is indeed an ant-hill, and these worlds are indeed this [ant-hill]; for the gods [placed him] within these worlds."
"Thus he contended with them; in this very way, he now contends with these worlds.
"Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns," [he says];
thus they sought him out during the dawns, and day after day, Jātavedas was the first.
"Thus they sought him on these days; 'and he has followed the rays of the sun,' thus they sought him in the rays of the sun;
'you have stretched yourself across heaven and earth,' thus they sought him in heaven and earth; they found him. In the very same way, this one now finds him when—when that [time]..."
He looks at the other [clay], then he covers it; they come to the clay.
6.3.3.[7] Then he consecrates the horse:
"The gods indeed said this: 'Let us drive away the evil from him. For fatigue is indeed evil."
"May we drive away the evil, the exhaustion of this [sacrifice].
Thus they drove away its evil, its exhaustion; in the same way, he now drives away this [sacrifice's] evil, its exhaustion.
"Having come, O steed, along the path. 6.3.3. [8]

"For his path has been reached; he shakes off all adversaries"—for "adversaries" (mṛdhaḥ) are indeed evils; thus, "he shakes off all evils. Therefore, when a horse has run its course, it shakes itself.
"In the great gathering-place, he desires to behold Agni with his eye"—this world, indeed, is that gathering-place.
"He gazes with his eye at Agni in this great assembly"—that is to say, in this great assembly. 6.3.3.
[9] Then he makes him step upon it;
for indeed, having discovered him (Agni) among the gods, he now makes him ascend.
He proclaimed, "It is here indeed! 6.3.3.[10] Furthermore, as to why he makes him step forward:
the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* or the *nāṣṭrās* [should seize] this one here."
Thinking, "They might strike [us]," they therefore made that horse their protector from above, even that yonder sun;
for this horse is indeed that sun. In the very same way, he now makes this horse his protector from above with this thunderbolt. "Having stepped forward, O steed... (ākramya vājin).

"Thou, with light, [beholding] the earth and Agni"—light is indeed sight; thus, "Thou, O steed, having stepped upon the earth and Agni with thy sight," he says this. "Having encompassed the ground, tell us where we may dig it up"—that is, "having probed the ground, tell us where we may dig it. 6.3.3. [12]
Then he strokes it;
for the gods, when he had spoken this, endowed him with vigor, and in the same way, this [priest] now endows him who has spoken this with vigor: "Heaven is thy..."

"The back is the earth, the seat is the atmosphere, the self is the ocean, the womb"—thus he says, "So art thou, so art thou. "Having looked around with thine eye, do thou trample upon those who attack," means, "Having looked around with thine eye, do thou trample upon all evils. He does not touch it, for it is indeed a thunderbolt.
"Lest this horse should injure me with the thunderbolt," [he thinks]. 6.3.3.
[13] Then he makes it step forward.
Regarding this, the gods said: "What shall we step upon as we step forward over this?"

"Great good fortune"—they caused him to step forward toward great good fortune; in the same way, this [priest] now causes him to step forward toward great good fortune. "Step forward for great good fortune"—that is, "step forward for your great good fortune. Therefore...
"This horse is the most fortunate of animals; from this place where you stand," [he says].

"O giver of wealth (*draviṇodā*)," for he indeed gives wealth to these [beings]. "O vigorous one (*vājin*)," for he is indeed vigorous. "May we be in the favor of the Earth, digging for Agni in her lap"—may we be in the favor of this Earth, digging for Agni in her lap.
"Digging," this refers to [the act of digging]. Then he addresses him as he departs:
"The gods indeed spoke thus to him when he had spoken, just as they would to one who has given."
Thus he pays homage, praising and magnifying him; in this very way, he now praises and magnifies him [with the words]:
"He has stepped forth. For he has indeed stepped forth. "The giver of wealth," for he gives wealth to these [people]. "The prize-winner, the steed," for he is both a prize-winner and a steed.
"He has made a fair world, a well-made one upon the earth," for he has indeed made a fair world, a well-made one.

"On the earth"—this means "then we shall dig. "The well-faced Agni"—this means "then we shall dig him. "Well-faced"—for Agni is well-faced on all sides. "Ascending to the highest vault"—the vault is indeed the heavenly world; thus, ascending to the heavenly world, [he says this] over it.

With the words, "The highest heaven," he leads it toward the south; where the other two animals are, they stand facing east on the south side. Whatever significance there is for the place on the south side in that [other] case, that same significance applies here.
Then, having sat down, he makes an offering over the clay.
The gods indeed said, "Reflect ye!"—that is to say, they said, "Seek ye a layer. While reflecting, they saw this oblation; having offered it, they saw these worlds as the fire-pan (ukhā). 6.3.3. [16]
They said, "Reflect! Indeed, they were saying, 'Seek a layer (citim icata)!

While reflecting, they saw this second oblation; having offered it, they saw these 'All-Lights' (viśvajyotis)—namely, these deities: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya; for these deities indeed are the All-light. In the very same way, the sacrificer [perceives] these two oblations."

Having offered these, he beholds these worlds and these deities; by offering with two interlinked [formulas], he interlinks both these worlds and these deities. Furthermore, as to why he offers these two oblations: 6.3.3 [17] And again, as to why he offers these two oblations.
He gratifies both the clay and those waters; having sacrificed to them and gratified them, he then gathers them together.
He offers with two intertwined [formulas]; thereby he intertwines the clay and the waters.
He offers with clarified butter.
Ghee is indeed a thunderbolt; he thus makes this thunderbolt his protector.

Moreover, ghee is seed; he thus pours forth seed. With the *sruva* ladle—he is a male, for the *sruva* is a male—and a male pours forth seed. With the utterance *svāhā*—he is a male, for the *svāhā* is a male—and a male pours forth seed. 6.3.3 [19]
"I sprinkle thee with mind and with ghee"— that is to say,
"I offer thee with both mind and ghee. "Dwelling facing all beings"— for he indeed dwells facing all beings.

"Broad, vast with transverse vigor"—for he is indeed broad and vast with transverse vigor by means of smoke; "most extensive, impetuous in food, visible"—that is to say, possessing space, an eater of food among foods, and shining. 6.3.3 [20]

"I besprinkle him who faces all directions" means "I offer oblation to him who faces everywhere. "May he enjoy that with a mind free from demons" means "may he take pleasure in that with a mind that is not ill-disposed. "He who is the glory of men, whose color is desirable..."
"Agni," [he says], for he is indeed the glory of men, "of longing color; Agni, flickering with his body, is not to be touched.
For he is indeed not to be touched while his body is blazing.
With two [verses] he makes the oblation.

The sacrificer has two feet; the sacrificer is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he pours him out as seed. With two verses addressed to Agni, he thus pours Agni himself out as seed.
In that they are addressed to Agni, it is Agni; and in that they are in the Triṣṭubh metre, it is Indra—for the sacrifice belongs to Indra and Agni.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he pours him out, having become seed. Indeed, Indra and Agni are all the gods;
Agni belongs to all the deities. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he pours him out, having become seed. 6.3.3 [22]
He offers an oblation in the footprint of the horse;
for this horse is Agni, and thus these two oblations of his become offered in Agni itself.
Then he traces a line around it.
He thus makes for him a measure, as it were, saying, "As great as you are.
Furthermore, as to why he draws a line around it: the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases*, the destroyers, [should seize] this one here."
"Lest they should strike him," he thought; therefore, they enclosed this stronghold for him. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now encloses this stronghold for himself.
The spade is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*); thus he makes the thunderbolt his protector. He traces it all around;
thus he makes that thunderbolt his protector from every side. He traces it three times.
He thus makes for him this threefold thunderbolt as a protector. "The lord of booty, the sage, [goes] around;
O Agni, we [take] thee as a fortress; thou, O Agni, by thy days"—[with these words] he [establishes] Agni for him.
Having praised this, he makes it into armor with the *parivati* verses; for the fortresses are surrounded, and by means of verses addressed to Agni, he thus makes this a fortress of fire for him.
Indeed, this fortress of fire stands blazing. He uses three verses; he thus makes this a triple fortress for him.
Therefore, the triple fortress is the supreme form of fortresses. And he does so with each succeeding metre being larger than the preceding one.

He makes one line after another more excellent; therefore, the lines of the fortresses become successively more excellent, for the lines are indeed the fortresses. 6.3.3.[26] Then he digs into this [earth] for him.

The gods were indeed afraid of this, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this [sacrifice] of ours. Therefore, they made this very [earth] their own self for protection, thinking, "The self will protect the self. It should be level with the rim; thus this earth becomes his own self. And as to why it is level with the rim: this [earth] is indeed the womb and this [offering] is the seed.
Whatever of the seed exceeds the womb, that becomes useless; and whatever is deficient, that is unsuccessful.
This, indeed, is the successful seed which is level and four-cornered. This [pit] becomes four-cornered, for there are four quarters;
he thus digs it from all the quarters. 6.4.1.1.
Then he digs for it from this very spot.
For the gods, having discovered it, dug for it; in the same way, this sacrificer, having discovered it, now digs for it: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ..."

"With the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, from the seat of the Earth, I dig for Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he digs for this Agni, who is favorable to cattle, from the lap of the Earth with these deities, just as Agni himself would do. 6.4.1. [2]
"O Agni, thee, the luminous one with a beautiful countenance"—for this Agni is indeed luminous and has a beautiful countenance;
"shining with undecaying luster"—that is to say, blazing with an imperishable flame; "harmless toward offspring."

"From the common seat of the earth, we dig for Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras"— this means "we dig for Agni, who is beneficial to offspring, non-injurious, and favorable to cattle, from the lap of the earth, in the manner of Agni. He digs with two verses.
The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus digs him up.
Moreover, this form consists of two things: clay and water.
He digs while saying, "I dig, I dig."
"Prajāpati dug it up, thinking, 'I dig';
the gods dug it up, thinking, 'We dig. Therefore one says, 'I dig,' or 'We dig. He digs with a spade.

"I dig with speech, I dig," he says; for the spade is indeed speech. This bamboo spade is made for the sake of a beginning. With this spade of speech, the gods dug him out; in the same way, he now digs him out with this spade of speech. 6.4.1. [6]
Then he collects it on a black antelope skin.

The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; thus he collects it on the sacrifice itself. It is with the hair-side up, for the hair are the meters; thus he collects it on the meters. He spreads it out silently.
The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; Prajāpati is the sacrifice, and Prajāpati is undefined. Its significance lies in its being placed to the north.
It has its neck toward the east, for that is the way of the gods.
Then he gathers it upon a lotus leaf.
The lotus leaf is indeed the womb; he pours that seed into the womb.
For whatever seed is poured into the womb becomes capable of procreation. He spreads it out with a mantra; the mantra is speech, and the lotus leaf is speech. 6.4.1 [8]
"You are the back of the waters, the womb of Agni"—
for this is indeed the back of the waters and the womb of Agni; "swelling around the ocean"— for this indeed swells on every side, increasing.

"Great indeed, O lotus!"—thus growing, "thou shalt increase, O lotus!"—with these words he strokes [the fire-altar]. "By the measure and the width of heaven, thou shalt extend"—he thus smooths it over.
For this Agni is yonder sun; no one other than heaven is able to encompass its width. "Having become heaven, grant us this [earth]," he says by this very act. 6.4.1. [9]
After that, he spreads out a black antelope skin;

the black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice, and this earth is the black antelope skin, for this earth is the sacrifice, since upon it the sacrifice is performed. The lotus leaf is the sky; the sky is indeed the waters, and the waters [are the lotus leaf].
"That upper one is indeed a lotus leaf.
Then he touches them both; by this, he effects a mutual recognition between the two, saying: "You two are a refuge and you two are a shield."
"For these two are his shelter and his impenetrable, wide shield"—for these two are indeed impenetrable and wide;
"dwell together, spacious ones"—that is, "dwell together, providing room"; "bear Agni Purīṣya"—that is, "bear Agni who is beneficial to cattle. 6.4.1. [11]
"Dwell together, you two who find the light; united by chest and by self"—this means "dwell together with him, you two who find the light, united by chest and by self.
"Bearing within you Agni, the luminous and unaging"—for that [luminous one] is indeed the sun.
"This is Agni; he is this very one, the luminous and the unaging; these two carry him within themselves. Therefore he says, 'The luminous and the unaging. [6.4.1.12] He touches it with two verses.

The sacrificer has two feet, and Agni is the sacrificer; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he thus establishes a common designation between these two. Moreover, this form is indeed twofold: the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf.

Then he touches the lump of clay with the words, "Thou art of the soil," which means "thou art favorable to cattle"; "the all-supporter," for he indeed supports all this; "Atharvan was the first to churn thee forth, O Agni," for Atharvan is indeed the breath, and the breath is indeed [Agni].
He churned him forth first with the words, "Thou art he who was created first as Agni";
thus he says this, and thereby he makes him that very one.
Then he encloses him.

With a spade on the south side and with his hand on the north side, [he says]: "From the lotus, O Agni, Atharvan churned thee forth. The lotus is indeed the waters; Atharvan is the breath. For the breath indeed churned him forth from the waters at the beginning. "From the head of the whole world, O worshipper"—this refers to the head of this entire universe.
Thus [ends section] 6.4.2.[3].
"The seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindled thee"—Vāc indeed is Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; he [kindled] this [Agni].
Then he kindled him with the verse, "The slayer of Vṛtra, the breaker of forts. Vṛtra is indeed evil; thus it means "the slayer of evil, the breaker of forts.
And you, O bull, [was kindled] by Pāthya.
"With fuel, he kindled the greatest slayer of Dasyus"—Pāthya Vṛṣan is indeed the mind; he kindled him from there.
"The winner of wealth in battle after battle"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*).
With *gāyatrī* verses.
The Gāyatrī is breath; he thus bestows breath upon this [sacrificer]. There are nine feet in those [verses];

there are indeed nine vital breaths. With seventy [syllables], there are three breaths—the out-breath (prāṇa), the up-breath (udāna), and the through-breath (vyāna)—and he places these very ones in him.
Two [feet] are directed downward in the head; he places these very ones in him. 6.4.2. [6]
Now these two subsequent [verses] are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the self; by means of these two, he prepares his very self.
"Sit down, O Hotṛ, in your own place, being observant"—the Hotṛ is indeed Agni, and this is his own place.
‘That black antelope skin which the wise one [wears]’—this means ‘the one who knows. ‘Settle the sacrifice in the womb of good action’—for the black antelope skin is indeed the womb of good action.
‘O God-favoring one, worship the gods with the oblation’—this means ‘being a god yourself, as a carrier of the gods, worship the gods with the oblation.
‘O Agni, bestow great vigor upon the sacrificer’—thus he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer. 6.4.2. [7]
"He has sat down as the Hotṛ-priest on the Hotṛ’s seat, knowing [the rite].

Agni is indeed the Hotṛ; the black antelope skin is the Hotṛ’s seat. "Knowing" means "knowing [the ritual]. "The brilliant, shining, and very skillful one has sat down. "Brilliant" means "shining"; "very skillful" means [possessing] great dexterity.
"Thus Vasiṣṭha, whose wisdom has unfailing vows"—for this Vasiṣṭha indeed has unfailing vows;
"Agni, the bearer of a thousand, the pure-tongued"—a thousand is indeed everything, so "the pure-tongued Agni is the bearer of everything.
With these two *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni, the significance has been explained. 6.4.2. [8]
Now, this last verse is a Bṛhatī.

Indeed, when it has been piled up, it attains the state of a Bṛhatī. For just as the seed is cast into the womb, so does that which is born come into being; since he makes this [last verse] a Bṛhatī here, therefore this [Agni], once piled up, becomes a Bṛhatī.
It attains the Bṛhatī metre. [He recites:
"Sit down; thou art great.
He thereby settles this very emitted seed within the womb. Therefore, the seed [is settled] in the womb.

"If sprinkled, it sinks down; grieve, O best invoker of the gods"—this means "shine forth, O best invoker of the gods. "O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, emit your ruddy smoke, O praised one, beautiful to behold"—for when he is kindled, he emits ruddy smoke that is indeed beautiful to behold, for he appears as if visible. 6.4.2. [10]
These amount to six;
the year consists of six seasons, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become; and furthermore, it is because he attains the year.

It attains the Bṛhatī metre, for the year is indeed the Bṛhatī: there are twelve full-moon nights, twelve Aṣṭakās, and twelve new-moon nights; that makes thirty-six, and the Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables. He brings it from the south towards the north, for seed is poured from the south into the womb from the north; this is its womb at this time, and he brings it without interruption for the sake of the seed.
‘For the sake of separation’ (VS 6.4.3).
Then he pours water there;
for whatever of this [clay] is injured or broken, that is joined together by means of water.
By means of the waters alone, he joins together and heals this wound and fissure of his. 6.4.3.
[2] "Release the divine waters, full of sweetness, for the health of offspring"—sweetness is indeed sap.
"For the sake of the subjects' freedom from consumption, [I take you] to the *rasavatī* river"—this refers to those [waters].
"From their place of standing, let the plants with good fruit rise up"—for indeed, from the place of standing of the waters, the plants with good fruit rise up.
6.4.3. Then he unites it with the wind.
Or rather, whatever of this [body] is wounded or torn apart by the wind—that is joined together by the wind;
by means of the wind itself, he thus extends and joins together this wound and tear of hers.
"May Vāyu Mātariśvan join you together," [he says].
This indeed is Vāyu Mātariśvan who blows here;

"the heart of her who lies extended, which has been rent asunder"—for this heart of hers, lying extended, has indeed been rent asunder; "thou who movest with the breath of all the gods"—for he moves with the breath of all the gods; "to which god, O God, let there be *vaṣaṭ*!"
"To thee!"—Prajāpati indeed is Ka; it is to him that he thus offers this Vaṣaṭ-call. There is no other oblation equal to this one.
Then he unites it with the quarters.
Or rather, whatever of this [earth] is wounded or torn apart is joined together by the quarters;
indeed, it is by means of the quarters that he heals this wound and tear of hers, unites it, and joins it together.
He joins these two quarters together, and therefore these two quarters are joined; and he joins these two [other] quarters together, and for that very reason these two also are joined.
"Thus first, then, then, then"—it turns to the right, for that is the way among the gods. By this [formula], medicine is prepared;
by this very means he heals her.
Then he takes up both the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf together.
The lotus leaf is indeed the womb;
by means of the womb, it receives the seed that has been poured out. Therefore, the seed poured out is received by the womb.

"Well-born, together with light, he has sat down in the shelter and protection, in heaven"—for he is indeed well-born, and this [lotus leaf] is both the shelter and the protection, together with light.
And he sits down.
6.4.3 [7] Then he girds him.
He thus joins that seed in the womb; therefore the seed joined in the womb does not fall away.
With a cord, for they yoke with a cord; with one made of muñja grass, triple-stranded—the significance of this has been explained.
6.4.3 [8] He wraps it around with the verse:
"O Agni, Vibhāvasu, clothe yourself in the multiform garment. For in the sacrifice, that which belongs to Varuṇa—
Having thus made him subject to the rope, he causes him to put on [the garment] just as one would cause a garment to be put on; so he causes him to put it on.
Then, taking hold of him, he rises up.
Yonder sun is indeed this fire; he thereby causes that sun to rise upward. 6.4.3. [9]

"Stand firm at the sacrifice"—for the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; "stand up, O thou worthy of fair sacrifice"—this is what it means; "protect us with divine wisdom"—that which is thy divine wisdom, with that protect us; "shining brightly with great light for us to see"—that is, shining brightly with great light so that we may see; "O Agni, come hither with fair praises"—those who are the bearers [of the oblation] are the "fair praises," O Agni.
"By those bearers"—this is [the meaning of] 6.4.3.[10].
Then he holds him up from here toward the east.
This Agni is indeed yonder sun; [he holds him up] toward yonder [sun].
He thus places that sun here upwards and facing eastward; therefore, yonder sun is placed here upwards and facing eastward.
With the words, "Stand up erect for our protection like the god Savitṛ," as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu).
With the words, "Erect, a winner of booty," he stands erect and wins booty—that is, food.
With the words, "When we invoke him with ointments and with singers," the rays are indeed his ointments and the singers; he thus addresses them.
He holds [the pole] over his head, for he is beyond the reach of this world. Then he lowers it;
having lowered it, he holds it above the navel; the significance of that has been explained above. 6.4.4. [1]
This is the hand; then he consecrates the animals.

For when the gods were about to collect these [animals], they first placed vigor within them; in the same way, this sacrificer, being about to collect them, now places vigor within them at the outset.
He consecrates the horse with the mantra:
"Thou art born as a fetus of the two worlds. These two worlds, heaven and earth, are indeed called *rodasī*;
he is born as their fetus. "O Agni, thou art beautiful, distributed among the plants"—for he is indeed beautiful, distributed among all plants.

"The variegated infant goes around the darknesses, the nights"—for this variegated infant indeed shines beyond the darknesses, the nights. "Crying out, he goes forth from his mothers"—the plants are indeed his mothers;
crying out, he goes forth from them. Thus he bestows vigor upon the horse.
Then [he addresses] the donkey:
"Be firm, O strong-limbed one; be swift, O vigorous steed. This means: "Be firm and strong-limbed, and be swift and a vigorous steed. "Be broad, you who are easy to sit upon for Agni."
"O carrier of dung, become broad and well-horned; you are the carrier of cattle for Agni"—this he says, thereby bestowing vigor upon the donkey.
Then [he addresses] the goat: "Be a crest for human offspring, O Aṅgiras! For Agni is indeed Aṅgiras, and he belongs to Agni.
"Jaḥ!"—this indeed pacifies it for the sake of non-injury. "Do not burn heaven and earth! Do not [burn] the atmosphere!
Do not [burn] the trees!"—this means "do not harm all this. Thus he bestows vigor upon the goat.
He consecrates it with three verses.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows vigor upon these [bricks].
Then he holds it up above these animals.

Therefore, he collects this [altar] with these animals, but he does not touch it. For animals are a thunderbolt and this [altar] is seed; [he does so] thinking, "Lest I injure this seed with the thunderbolt. Furthermore, [he thinks], "This is Agni and these are the animals;
lest this Agni injure these animals. 6.4.4. [7]
He holds [the grass] over the horse with the verse, "Let the steed go forth neighing. "Let the steed go forth neighing" means "let the steed go forth while being made to neigh";
"the ass brays loudly as he flies" (nānadadrāsabhaḥ patvā)—thereby, in the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) for the horse, he excludes the ass; thus, he places the affliction (*śuc*) upon the ass.

"He bears Agni Purīṣya; may he not fall before his full span of life"—by saying this, "bearing Agni who is beneficial to cattle, may he not fall before this rite," he thus collects him with the horse.
Now [the verse] for the donkey:
"Carrying Agni, the bull, the bull"—for Agni is indeed a bull and the donkey is a bull; thus that bull carries the bull.
"The embryo of the waters, belonging to the ocean"—for he is indeed the embryo of the waters and belongs to the ocean; thus he collects him with the donkey. 6.4.4. [9]

Then he draws it out with the verse, "O Agni, come for the feast" (*agna āyāhi vītaye*); "for the feast" (*vītaye*) means "for the enjoyment" (*avitave*). Thus, by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), the sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he draws him out from this class of the Sudra. 6.4.4 [10]
Now as for the goat: "Right (ṛta), truth (satya); right, truth. This fire, indeed, is the right; yonder sun is the truth. Or rather, yonder [sun] is the right and this [fire] is the truth;
for this fire is both. Therefore he says, "Right, truth; right, truth," and thus he prepares it with the goat. 6.4.4. [11]

He gathers with three [verses]. Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus gathers him. He consecrates them beforehand with three [verses]; that makes six; the significance of that has been explained. 6.4.4. [12]

Then they turn these animals back; of them, the goat goes first, then the donkey, then the horse. Now, from here, when they go forth, the horse goes first, then the donkey, then the goat. The horse indeed follows the Kṣatriya, while the donkey and the goat follow the Vaiśya and the Śūdra.
And following [the horse] are the donkey and the goat.
6.4.4. [13] Therefore, since the horse goes first among those departing from here, therefore the Kṣatriya, going first, [is followed by] the other three.

The other three castes follow behind the Brāhmaṇa when he goes first from here toward that world; therefore, when a Brāhmaṇa goes first, the other three castes follow behind him. But when one does not go from here nor from there, the donkey goes first; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya never [follow] a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.

And because he follows after [the horse] from behind, they thus proceed without confusion; furthermore, by means of this, he encompasses these two social classes on both sides with the Brahman and the Kṣatra, making them inseparable.
6.4.4. Then he gazes at the Anaddhāpuruṣa.
"With 'We bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras,' he means 'we bear Agni, the source of cattle, like Agni.
Thus he collects him with the Unnamed Man (Anaddhāpuruṣa).
He goes along holding him above a goat.
The goat indeed belongs to Agni; he thus gathers it by means of its own self, its own deity.
Moreover, the goat is the Brahman; he thus gathers it by means of the Brahman.
Then he brings it down.

"O plants, rejoice at this auspicious Agni as he approaches you. For the plants are afraid of him as he approaches, thinking, "May he not harm us. He appeases him for their sake with the words, "Rejoice at him; he approaches you as one auspicious; he will not harm you."

"Driving away all deficiencies and diseases, sit down; drive away our ill-will"—that is to say, "driving away all deficiencies and diseases, sit down; drive away every evil. 6.4.4. [17] "O plants, receive [him]!"

"Bearing flowers, bearing good fruit"—this is indeed their perfect form, in that they bear flowers and bear good fruit; "May they receive him in perfection"—this is what he means. "This germ of yours, born in due season, has settled in its ancient dwelling"—this germ of yours, born in the seasons, has settled in its eternal abode.
"He has taken his seat together with [them]," so it is said. He brings it down with two verses;
the sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni—as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure.
He brings it down by that much alone; he brings it down from the south toward the north—the significance of this has been explained.

At the place where he brings it down, the ground is raised and sprinkled; for indeed, they establish the fire on ground that is both raised and sprinkled. Sand is scattered there; the significance of that is as follows. 6.4.4 [19]
It is enclosed on all sides.

For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this [Agni] here"; they therefore enclosed him within this fortress. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now encloses him within this fortress.
He encloses it; for this earth is indeed the womb and this [clay] is the seed. Indeed, the seed is poured as if in secret within the womb;
thus this is made into the form of a womb. Therefore, even with one's own wife, one desires to behave as if in secret.
Then he unbinds it.
Whatever part of him, while he is thus bound, becomes singed, that very impurity he thereby places outside of himself; moreover, he causes him to be born from this very womb.
"Flaming with broad radiance... (RV 10.88.1).

"Shining forth with broad radiance"—this means that; "drive away the haters, the Rākṣasas, and diseases"—this means "drive away all evils"; "may we be in the protection of the great, well-protecting Agni, under the guidance of the one who dwells with us"—with these words he invokes a blessing. 6.4.4. [22]
Then, having gathered the goat's hair, he lets the animals loose toward the north-east;
for this direction, the north-east, belongs to both gods and men, and it is in that direction he places the animals; therefore both gods and men [partake] thereof.
They subsist on livestock. These waters have been boiled with a decoction of *parṇa* leaves; this is indeed for the sake of stability, and as for why they are boiled with a *parṇa* decoction—
The *parṇa* tree is indeed Soma, and Soma is indeed the moon;
this is one form of Agni. It is for the attainment of this very form of Agni that he pours them out. 6.5.1 [2] He pours them out.

"O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss. For whatever deity a *ṛc* verse refers to, and whatever deity a *yajus* formula refers to, that is the deity of that *ṛc* and that is the deity of that *yajus*. This triplet of verses is those very Waters;
for those waters which appeared as a single form, it is that very form he thereby produces.
Then, having produced foam, he places it upon [the clay].
That which was produced as the second form, namely the foam—that very form he now makes. And the clay which he mixes therein is that very clay; this is the third [form].
"Form was created from these"—for indeed, in the beginning, he (the sacrificer) was created from these forms; it is from those very forms that he now causes him to be born. 6.5.1 [4].
Then he mixes it with goat's hair. This is for the sake of stability; and as to why he uses goat's hair—it was from the animals that the gods [obtained this].
In the same way that they then gathered it together from the goats, so now he gathers this together from the cattle.
As to why with goat-hair: for in the goat is the form of all cattle; and as to why hair—for hair is indeed form. 6.5.1. [5] Having mixed it together, Mitra...

"Earth and ground together with light"—Mitra is indeed breath; it was breath that performed this work at the beginning. "The well-born Jātavedas—for the sake of health I unite thee for offspring"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. 6.5.1. [6]
Then these three things become ground together: sugar, stone, and iron filings; with these he mixes [the clay] for the sake of stability.
And as to why he does so with these: this earth was created in such a measure at the beginning; thus, it is with as much as this earth was created at the beginning that he mixes it.
In this way, he makes her just as large as that.
"The Rudras, having mixed the earth, have kindled the great light"—for yonder sun is indeed this Agni; this is what [the verse means]. 6.5.1. [7]
"The Rudras, having mixed the earth, kindled the great light; their unceasing, bright radiance shines among the gods. Indeed, this is their unceasing, bright radiance that shines among the gods.
He mixes [the earth] with two [verses].
The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus mixes him.
Then he stirs it together.

"May she be united with the Vasus and the Rudras"—for she is indeed united with both the Vasus and the Rudras; that which is with Mitra is with the Vasus, and that which is with the Rudras is with the Rudras. "The clay fit for the work"—for they are wise, and this clay is fit for the work.
Having made it soft with his two hands, [he says], "May Sinīvālī fashion it. Vāc (Speech) is indeed Sinīvālī.

"Having made her soft with both hands, let him fashion her"—this is what is meant. "Sinīvālī, with beautiful braids, with a beautiful head-dress, with beautiful ornaments"—Sinīvālī is indeed a woman; this is indeed [the praise] of a woman. 6.5.1.[10]
"May she who has beautiful braided hair, beautiful head-dress, and fine ornaments, prosper her form;
may she, O Aditi, place the fire-pan (ukhā) for thee, the great one, in her hands. This earth, indeed, is Aditi; it is to her that he says this.
"Let her fashion the fire-pan."
"By power, by the two arms, Aditi, through wisdom"—for indeed she acts by power, by the two arms, and by wisdom; "as a mother bears her son in her lap, so let her bear Agni as her embryo.
Just as a mother would bear her son in her lap, so let her bear Agni in her womb—this is what it means. 6.5.1 [12]
He mixes it with three [verses]. Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus mixes him.
He combines [the earth] with two [verses]; that makes five. The fire-altar consists of five layers; the year has five seasons; the year is Agni.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. He pours water over it with three verses; thus it becomes eightfold.

The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. Moreover, this earth was created in the beginning as consisting of eight syllables; thus, it becomes as great as this earth was created in the beginning.
In this way, he makes it exactly that large.
6.5.2.1. Then he takes a lump of clay, as much as is sufficient for the *nidhi* (the treasure-vessel), [with the formula]: "Thou art the head of Makha. The sacrifice, indeed, is Makha.
The head of Makha is this Āhavanīya fire; for the Āhavanīya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and he is about to pile up that very [fire-altar].
Therefore he says, "Thou art the head of Makha. Furthermore, as to why he says, "Thou art the head of Makha":
This [Agni] is born when he is piled; for one who is being born is born from the head and from the mouth.
[He piles him] thinking, "May he be born from the head and from the mouth as he is being born.
He spreads him out.
"May the Vasus fashion you with the Gāyatrī metre, like Aṅgiras"—this world here is indeed that treasure;

the Vasus fashioned it with the Gāyatrī metre, and in the same way, he now fashions this [brick] with the Gāyatrī metre. "Like Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras is indeed the breath; "Thou art firm"—that is to say, "Thou art steady. Furthermore...

"Thou art established," [he says]; "thou art the earth," for this earth is indeed a treasure-chest. "Bestow upon me offspring, abundance of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic vigor, and kinsmen for the sacrificer"—the Vasus, having fashioned this world, invoked this blessing therein; in the very same way, the sacrificer, having fashioned this world, [invokes it].

Over this, he pronounces this benediction: having made it a span in measure, he then raises its bank on all sides. 6.5.2. [4] Then he places the first layer: "May the Rudras fashion thee with the Triṣṭubh metre."

"Like Aṅgiras with the Canda metre"—the atmosphere is indeed this [layer], and it is the ocean; the Rudras made that with the Triṣṭubh metre, and in the same way he now makes it with the Triṣṭubh metre.
"Like Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras is indeed the breath—"thou art firm (dhruvā)"—that is, "thou art steady," and also "thou art established"; "thou art the atmosphere"—the atmosphere.

"May this ocean bear to me offspring, abundance of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic strength, and kinsmen for the sacrificer"—for the Rudras, having made the intermediate space, invoked this blessing therein;
in the very same way, the sacrificer, having made the intermediate space, invokes this blessing therein. Having smeared it together...
[5] Having smoothed it, he then places the upper wooden ring [on top], saying:
"May the Ādityas fashion you with the Jāgata metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras."

This is indeed the sky as the upper layer; the Ādityas fashioned it by means of the Jagatī metre, and in the same way, he now fashions it by means of the Jagatī metre. "Aṅgirasvat" (like Aṅgiras)—for Aṅgiras is indeed the breath—"dhruvāsī" (thou art firm); that is to say, "thou art steady," and also "thou art established. "Dyaurasi" (thou art the sky); for this [layer] is indeed the sky.

"O Uddhi, bestow upon me offspring, abundance of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic strength, and kinsmen for the sacrificer"—for it was thus that the Ādityas, having made the sky, invoked this blessing upon it;
in the very same way, the sacrificer, having made the sky, invokes this blessing upon it. 6.5.2. [6]
Then he performs with this fourth *yajus*:
"May the All-gods, the Vaiśvānaras, fashion thee with the *anuṣṭubh* metre, like Aṅgiras. For this *yajus* is indeed the quarters; these All-gods, the Vaiśvānaras, are in them.

With this fourth sacrificial formula, they placed the quarters within the fire-pan among these worlds; in the same way, the sacrificer now places the quarters within the fire-pan among these worlds with this fourth sacrificial formula. "Aṅgirasvat"—Aṅgiras is indeed the breath—"dhruvāsī" means "you are firm," and also "you are established. "Diśo 'si" (you are the quarters), for this sacrificial formula is indeed the quarters. "Dhārayā mayi" (support me).

"Progeny, increase of wealth, lordship of cattle, heroic vigor, and kinsmen for the sacrificer"—the All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ), who are common to all men (Vaiśvānarāḥ), having made the quarters their own, invoked this blessing upon them; in the very same way, the sacrificer, having made the quarters his own, invokes this blessing upon them. 6.5.2. [7]
Therefore, by means of this [formula], he makes it both from within and from without.
For this reason, he makes these worlds from within and from without, and by means of this [formula] he makes the quarters immeasurable; for the quarters are indeed immeasurable. 6.5.2.[8]
He makes it exactly a span high and a span wide across;
for Viṣṇu, as an embryo, is a span long, and this is his womb; thus he makes the womb commensurate with the embryo. 6.5.2 [9]
If it should be larger than a span, he should make it smaller by means of this *yajus*; if it should be smaller, he should make it larger by means of this. 6.5.2. [10]

If there should be one animal, he should make it one span; but if there should be five animals, he should make it five spans, or else the measure of an arrow; for strength is indeed like an arrow, and thus it becomes commensurate with strength.
"Indeed, it was formerly five spans wide in front," so they say.
Then he lays down a transverse girdle;
for this is indeed the quarters. For the gods, having made these worlds into a fire-pan (*ukhā*), [proceeded].

With the quarters they made it firm, and with the quarters they enclosed it; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made these worlds into the fire-pan (ukhā), makes them firm with the quarters and encloses them with the quarters.
He places it on the northern third.
"Here indeed the ends of these worlds meet;
it is there that he binds them. [He says:
"Thou art the girdle of Aditi."
For the rope at the sacrifice belongs to Varuṇa; having thus made this girth-band non-Vāruṇa, he spreads it around. Then he makes four upright [staves].

They remained silent; for these very quarters are indeed those [supports]. For the gods, having made these worlds into the fire-pan (*ukhā*), made them firm on all sides by means of the quarters; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made these worlds into the fire-pan, makes them firm on all sides by means of the quarters. 6.5.2. [15]
These [bricks] belong to this [altar].

For these [bricks] indeed supported it in the beginning, and in the same way they support it now. That part which is above is made firm by this one [the *tiraścī* brick], and that part which is below is made firm by these [other bricks]. 6.5.2. [16]
They raise the breasts at the front of these [cups].

For the gods, having made these worlds into a *ukhā* (fire-pan), milked all desires by means of these breasts; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made these worlds into a *ukhā*, [milks them] by means of these breasts.
"May she milk all desires.
(6.5.2.17) This very [fire-pan] is indeed a cow. These worlds are the fire-pan; these worlds are the cow. That which is this horizontal girdle is her udder.
It is at the third part [of the udder], for the cow is indeed milked at the third part.
He draws up her teats;
he draws up the teats from the udder, and she becomes four-teated, for she is indeed four-teated.
Regarding the cow [at Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.5.2.19]: some indeed make it two-teated, or even eight-teated; one should not do so, for such is the nature of the cow.

Animals with fewer udders are those that have more udders, yet these are less fit for subsistence for him; indeed, they make her less fit for subsistence, and moreover, they do not even make her a cow, but rather a bitch, a ewe, or a mare. Therefore, one should not do so. 6.5.2. [20]

Then he approaches its opening with the formula, "May Aditi grasp thy opening. Aditi is indeed speech; for having fashioned her thus, the gods established her by means of speech, Aditi. In the same way, this sacrificer, having fashioned her thus, now establishes her by means of speech, Aditi. 6.5.2. [21]
Having taken it up, he sets it down with the verse,
"Having made the great pan," which means "having made the large pan";
"the womb of Agni out of clay," for this womb of Agni is indeed made of clay.
"Aditi gave her to her sons, saying, 'Cook them! Indeed, Aditi, having made her thus, gave her to the gods, her sons, for the purpose of cooking;
and in the same way, this [priest], having made her thus, gives her to the gods for the purpose of cooking.
Some, indeed, make her threefold.

"These three worlds are these very worlds; the fire-pan (ukhā) is these worlds," so they say. Furthermore, they argue for one another's expiation: "If this one breaks, we shall carry the fire in that other one;
if that one breaks, we shall carry it in the other. One should not do so. For that which is this first treasure is this world, and that which is...
The first *uditi* is the intermediate space; that which is the second is the sky; and as for this fourth *yajus*, it is indeed the quarters.
Now, all this that exists is only as much as these worlds and the quarters. If he were to add anything here, he would cause an excess;
and whatever is done in excess at the sacrifice overflows upon the sacrificer’s hateful rival. Therefore...
The expiation for a [sacrificial post] that has split is explained later in the subsequent exposition (6.5.3).
For this very [post], he places the *aṣāḍhā* brick first;
for the *aṣāḍhā* is indeed this [earth], and she is one of these worlds.
The earth was created first; he makes it from this very clay, for this [earth] is the queen (mahiṣī) of these worlds. Indeed, she is the queen;
thus, that which was first found is the queen.
It is one foot in measure.
The foot is indeed a foundation; this earth is the foundation. It is marked with three lines, for this earth is threefold. 6.5.3.
[3] Now he makes the fire-pan (ukhā).
He thus creates these worlds; then he makes the Viśvajyotis bricks. These deities—Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—are indeed the universal light (viśvaṃ jyotiḥ). He makes them from this very same clay;
thus the sacrificer fashions these gods from these worlds. He makes them with three lines drawn upon them.
"For these gods are threefold"—this refers to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self (adhyātma):
the fire-pan (ukhā) is the self, and the Aṣāḍhā brick is speech; he places that first, for speech is placed in front of the self.
He makes the speech from this very clay, for this speech is indeed his own; he makes it a buffalo-cow, for speech is a buffalo-cow.

It is inscribed with a stylus, for speech is divided threefold: the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman*s. Moreover, these three are the forms of speech: in a whisper, in between, and aloud. 6.5.3. [5]
Then he makes the fire-pan (ukhā);

he thereby makes his own self. Then he makes the Viśvajyotis bricks; offspring indeed is the Viśvajyotis, for offspring is indeed the light of all; thus he effects procreation. These [bricks] are made from this very same clay.

The sacrificer makes it for himself; he fashions his offspring. The sacrificer makes it; the sacrificer makes it for himself. He makes it unseparated; he thus makes his offspring unseparated from himself. He makes it subsequent; he thus makes his offspring subsequent to himself. They are drawn with three lines, for procreation is threefold, as is the father.
The mother, the son, and then the embryo, the amnion, and the chorion—these he prepares with the *yajus* formulas;
the others he prepares without the *yajus*. These [first ones] are expressed, while the others remain unexpressed.
These [verses] are limited, while the others are unlimited.
This Agni is Prajāpati;
for Prajāpati is both defined and undefined.

It is both limited and unlimited. Those [bricks] which he lays down with a *yajus*-formula—for that which is his expressed, limited form, he thereby perfects it; and those which he lays down without a *yajus*-formula—for that which is his unexpressed, unlimited form, he thereby perfects it. Verily, he who does this perfects this Prajāpati in his entirety and completeness.
Knowing thus, he does this; then he leaves over a lump for the *upaśaya* (the lying-down brick) for the sake of expiations. 6.5.3 [8].
Then he fumigates it—for the sake of stability, and also to ensure the proper commencement of the rite; and as to why he fumigates it, it is the head.
The fire-pan (ukhā) is this [body] of the sacrifice; the smoke is the breath, and that is the head. Thus he bestows breath upon it. He fumigates it with horse-hairs.
The horse belongs to Prajāpati, and Agni is Prajāpati; surely the self does not [injure] the self.
He destroys it for the sake of non-injury; indeed, it is as if he had eaten it with a dog, for it is then spent and exhausted; thus he does not injure the horse, nor the other animals. 6.5.3.
"May the Vasus fumigate you!"
With the Gāyatrī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may the Rudras fumigate you;
with the Triṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may the Ādityas fumigate you; with the Jagatī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may the Viśve Devas, common to all men, fumigate you;
with the Anuṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may Indra fumigate you.
"May Varuṇa fumigate thee; may Viṣṇu fumigate thee"—with these very deities he thus fumigates it.
There are seven horse-hairs; there are seven sacrificial formulas; these deities are sevenfold; there are seven vital breaths in the head. Why...

Or even many times—seven times each, seven indeed; he thereby bestows the seven vital breaths upon its head. 6.5.4.[1] Then he digs it into this earth. For the gods were afraid, thinking: "Lest the *rakṣases* and *nāṣṭrās* [should seize] this one here."
"Lest they should kill it," [he thinks]; therefore, by making this very earth its body, "the body will protect the body through protection.
6.5.4. [2] He digs it with an Aditi [spade].
Aditi is indeed this earth; for one does not harm oneself, so [he uses this] for the sake of non-injury, rather than with another [tool].
If one digs with a deity [in mind], one would injure him.
"May the goddess Aditi, favored by all the gods,
dig thee down in the lap of the earth like Aṅgiras, O pit!"— thus for the pit.

This is indeed that bamboo splinter which settles here among the gods; this pit becomes four-cornered, for there are four quarters, and thus he digs it from all the quarters. Then, having placed the supporting layer, he lays down the *aṣāḍhā* brick silently, for he makes that one first. 6.5.4. [4]
Then he places the fire-pan (ukhā) [on the hearth], saying:

"May the divine wives of the gods, who are accompanied by all the gods, place thee, O pan, in the lap of the earth, in the manner of the Aṅgirases. For in the beginning, those divine wives of the gods, who were accompanied by all the gods, [placed it] on the earth.
"In the common dwelling, like Aṅgiras"—with those very [bricks] he thus places her. Those indeed are the plants;
for the wives of the gods are the plants, since by means of the plants all this is supported here; with the plants he thus places her. Then he lays down the Viśvajyotis bricks silently, and then...
Having placed the cooking vessel, he kindles it [with the verse]:
"May the goddesses Dhiṣaṇās, accompanied by all the gods, kindle you in the seat of the earth, like Aṅgiras. 6.5.4. [5]

Thus, in the beginning, the goddesses Dhiṣaṇās, accompanied by all the gods, kindled her upon the seat of the earth in the manner of Aṅgiras; with those very [Dhiṣaṇās] he now kindles her. She is indeed Speech; for Dhiṣaṇā is Speech, since by Speech all this is kindled; it is with Speech that he thus kindles her. Then, while looking [at her], he mutters these three sacrificial formulas. 6.5.4. [6]
"O Varūtrīs, goddesses, accompanied by all the gods, may you cause the fire-pan to swell in the dwelling-place of the earth, as did Aṅgiras"— for indeed, in the beginning,
those Varūtrīs, the goddesses, accompanied by all the gods, caused it to swell in the dwelling-place of the earth, as did Aṅgiras.

With those very [verses] he thus causes her to be cleansed; for those are indeed the days and nights, for the *varūtris* are the days and nights, since by means of the days and nights all this is encompassed;
it is with the days and nights that he thus causes her to be cleansed.
"May the divine *gnās* [cleanse] thee."

"May they cook in the lap of the earth, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, like Aṅgiras, O pot!"—for in the beginning, the divine Gnas, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, cooked this in the lap of the earth like Aṅgiras; with them he now cooks it. These are indeed the meters; for the meters are indeed [the Gnas].
For the *gnās* go to the heavenly world by means of the meters; with the meters he thus cooks her.
"O divine Mothers, whose wings are cut off, accompanied by all the gods, [cook her] in the dwelling-place of the earth."

"Like Aṅgiras, cook her in the pan!"—for in the beginning, these divine women, the stars, who have broad leaves and are favored by all the gods, cooked her on the seat of the earth like Aṅgiras; with those very ones he now cooks her.
And they are indeed the stars; for the stars are the women, since those people who perform meritorious deeds go to the heavenly world.
These are their lights; he thus cooks her by means of the constellations (nakṣatras).
He digs with one [verse], places [the material] with one, kindles [the fire] with one, cooks with one, and [removes it] with two.

He cooks it; therefore, food ripens twice in a year. These amount to six; the year has six seasons, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become. 6.5.4. [10] Then [he recites]: "O Mitra, supporter of the people..."

He proceeds with the *mitra* formula; however much he proceeds, neither does *mitra* harm anyone, nor does anyone harm *mitra*. In the same way, he does not harm this [earth], nor does she harm him. He should strew it during the day and remove it during the day, for the day belongs to Agni. 6.5.4. [11]
He digs it up with a Yajus formula addressed to Savitṛ.
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he digs it up.
"May the god Savitṛ dig you up—well-handed, well-fingered, well-armed, and also powerful," he says, for all this is indeed Savitṛ.
Then he turns it over with the words:
"Unswerving on the earth, fill the regions and the quarters. This means: "Unswerving, do thou fill the regions and the quarters on the earth with sap. 6.5.4. [13]
Then he lifts it up:
"Rising, become great," for these worlds, having risen, are indeed great; "Arise, thou art firm," that is to say, "Arise, thou art steadfast and established. 6.5.4. [14]
Having taken hold of it, he sets it down:
"O Mitra, I entrust this pan to you, so that it may not break; let it not shatter.
Vāyu, who blows here, is indeed Mitra; it is to him that he thus entrusts it for protection. These, then, are the worlds.
"Therefore, these worlds are protected by friends; nothing of them is lost.
Then he moistens it.
This is for stability, and also so that the ritual action may proceed from its beginning. Furthermore, as to why he moistens it: [it is] the head.
The fire-pan (ukhā) is this very sacrifice; the milk is the vital breath (prāṇa), and the head is the vital breath. Thus, he bestows the vital breath. Moreover, the fire-pan is indeed a woman;
he thus places the milk in a woman, and therefore milk is found in a woman.
He mixes it with the milk of a she-goat.

From the grief of Prajāpati, indeed, the she-goat was born; Prajāpati is Agni, and one does not injure one's own self. It is for the sake of non-injury. Furthermore, as for the she-goat: the she-goat eats all plants; he thus anoints her with the sap of all those plants. 6.5.4. [17]

May the Vasus moisten you with the Gāyatrī metre, after the manner of Aṅgiras; may the Rudras moisten you with the Triṣṭubh metre, after the manner of Aṅgiras; may the Ādityas moisten you with the Jagatī metre, after the manner of Aṅgiras; [may] the Viśve Devas [moisten you].

"May the Vaiśvānara fires roar after her with the Anuṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras"—with these very deities he thus makes her roar. Indeed, by whichever deities he performs the work, by those same ones he fumigates it and by those same ones he makes it roar; for whoever performs a ritual action, he alone knows the proper procedure for it.
Therefore, with the very same deities by which he performs [the sacrifice], he fumigates it and with them he cuts it. 6.6.1.
There are more sacrificial oblations;
for there are rites both in the piling of the fire-altar and those that are not.

Those other rites which he transcends—namely the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), the Rājasūya, the Vājapeya, and the Aśvamedha—because he transcends those other rites, they are called "transcended" (*atīni*). 6.6.1.
[2] There is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu.
The *dīk�ṣaṇīyā* offering for that sacrifice consists of a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and a pap for Āditya; these belong to Agni. 6.6.1.
[3] Now, if he were to offer only the oblation to Agni-Viṣṇu...

If the other two oblations were offered, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* would belong only to the *adhvara* sacrifice and not to Agni; and if one were to offer only the other two oblations, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* would belong only to Agni and not to the *adhvara*. 6.6.1. [4]
He offers both:
for this rite belongs to both the Adhvara and Agni; it is both an Adhvara rite and an Agni rite. First that of the Adhvara, then that of Agni, for the Agni rite is subsidiary to this rite. 6.6.1. [5]
As for this offering to Agni and Viṣṇu,
its Brāhmaṇa explanation is the same as that for the preliminary rite;
there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara, for Vaiśvānara is indeed all the fires, and it serves for the attainment of all the fires.
The cake is on twelve potsherds; there are twelve months in a year, and Vaiśvānara is the year. Furthermore, when he offers this Vaiśvānara oblation, he is about to generate this Agni Vaiśvānara.
He pours this [oblation] as seed into the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering before [the main sacrifice]. For whatever kind of seed is poured into the womb, such is what is born;
since he pours this Vaiśvānara here as seed, therefore he is born there as Vaiśvānara. 6.6.1. [7]
Furthermore, as to why he offers these two oblations:

Vaiśvānara is the nobility (*kṣatra*), and this *caru* for the Ādityas is the common people (*viś*). Thus, he establishes both the nobility and the common people. He offers the Vaiśvānara oblation first; having thus established the nobility, he provides for the common people. 6.6.1 [8]
This one [oblation] has a single deity; it makes that kṣatra concentrated in one place and makes prosperity concentrated in one place.
The other is a *caru* with many deities; this *caru* is indeed a multiplicity of rice grains, and the Ādityas among the gods are a multiplicity within the *viś*.
"He bestows that abundance"—this refers to the deities (adhidevatam).
Now, with reference to the self (adhyātmam): Vaiśvānara is indeed the head, and this *caru* offering is the Āditya; thus it is both the head and the self.
He prepares the Vaiśvānara [oblation]; he offers it first. Having thus made the head, he makes the body.
This one [offering] is single;
for the head is, as it were, single. The other is a pap (caru) for many deities; for this is the abundance of rice-grains.
That which is the caru is the abundance of the limbs; that which is the self is the abundance of the limbs. Thus he bestows abundance upon the limbs.
It is made with ghee, for the Ādityas have ghee as their portion; he thus satisfies them with their own portion, with their own essence.
He gratifies [the gods]; these oblations are performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Indeed, seed is here in the sacrifice, and seed is indeed poured out in a low voice. 6.6.1.
Then he offers the *audgrabhaṇa* oblations.
By means of the *audgrabhaṇa* oblations, the gods [ascended] from this world to the heavenly world.

They lifted up the world; because they lifted it up (*udagṛhṇata*), they are called *audgrabhaṇa* offerings. In the same way, the sacrificer now, by means of the *audgrabhaṇa* offerings, lifts himself up from this world toward the heavenly world.
These [offerings] are indeed numerous.
Whether it be in the case of the piling of the fire-altar or when there is no piling of the fire-altar, its significance has already been stated.

There are both types; their significance has already been stated. First come those of the *adhvara* sacrifice, and then those of the fire-altar; their significance has likewise already been stated. He offers five oblations of the *adhvara*.

The sacrifice is fivefold; as great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is—with just that much he pours this [seed] into it once it has become semen. There are seven [verses] for Agni; Agni consists of seven layers;
there are seven seasons in the year; the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he pours this [seed] into it once it has become semen.
He pours those two together; they amount to twelve. There are twelve months in a year, and Agni is the year.
As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become.
6.6.1. He offers: "To Ākūti, to Agni, to the Impulse, Svāhā! For from Ākūti, indeed, this rite first proceeds.
That very thing became this; he employs it for this rite:
"Mind, the impulse, Agni the impeller—Svāhā!
For this is the first action of the mind.
That very thing became this; he employs it for this rite:
"Citta, the known, Agni, the impeller—Svāhā!
For from Citta, indeed, this rite first proceeded.
That very thing became this; he employs it for this rite:
"To Vāc’s support, to Agni the impeller, Svāhā!
For this is indeed the first act of speech.
It became equal; he employs it for this very rite with the formula, "To Prajāpati Manu, svāhā!
Prajāpati indeed is Manu, for he has reflected upon (amanuta) all this.
Prajāpati indeed performed this rite first; he now employs it for this very rite:
"To Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā!
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; the year, indeed, performed this first.
Savitṛ indeed performed this very rite in the beginning; he now employs it for this very purpose. Then he offers the Sāvitrī oblation;
Savitṛ indeed performed this very rite in the beginning; he now employs it for this very purpose.
Every mortal man employs the friendship of the god who is the leader; every man seeks wealth, let him choose glory that he may prosper.
"Svāhā!"—he who chooses the friendship of the god Savitṛ chooses both glory and prosperity.
He who performs this rite chooses his friendship. 6.6.1 [22]

Now, some indeed offer these Audgrabhaṇa oblations into the fire-pan itself, saying: "These are offered for the sake of desires; this fire-pan is the self of the sacrificer; thus we establish all the desires of the sacrificer within his own self."

One should not do so; for when this sacrifice has been completed, that which is the essence of these oblations is this very flame that shines forth. When the sacrifice is completed and the *audgrabhaṇa* offerings have been made, he then covers the *ukhā* pot;
thus this sacrifice mounts it and sustains that sacrifice. Therefore, [he should do so] only when the sacrifice has been completed.
When the *audgrabhaṇa* offerings have been offered, one should heat the *ukhā* pot.
It is strewn with a tuft of *muñja* grass;
it is indeed for the purpose of kindling it, and furthermore, because of the tuft of *muñja* grass.
The muñja grass is the womb of Agni; indeed, the womb does not harm the embryo, for the sake of non-injury. For one who is being born is born from a womb;
[he thinks], "May he be born from a womb as he is being born. There is an inner layer of hemp. 6.6.1. [24]

"He shall kindle [the fire]," he says; for indeed, when Prajāpati was emitted from that womb, its caul was *umā* and its afterbirth was *caṇā*. Therefore, those are foul-smelling, for they are indeed the afterbirth. The afterbirth does not harm the embryo; it is for the sake of non-injury. Verily, one who is born is born with an afterbirth; being born with an afterbirth, he is born.
"May you be born," [he says].
6.6.2.[1] He applies it while standing; for these worlds are indeed the fire-pan, and these worlds are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is most powerful. 6.6.2.[2]
Standing facing north-east;
for standing facing north-east, Prajāpati created offspring.
And furthermore, as to why he stands facing north-east:
For this direction, which is north-east, belongs to both gods and men. Moreover,
because the door to the heavenly world is in that direction, he stands facing north-east.
Standing, he offers the oblations; standing facing north-east, he leads [the victim] toward the south. Thus, by means of the very gate, he causes him to reach the treasure of the heavenly world.
"Do not break! Do not be harmed! [he says].

"As the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its symbolic explanation (bandhu): 'O Mother, be bold and act as a hero! For the fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed a woman, and 'Mother' is a term of address for a woman. 'Be as if a hero' means: 'Agni and you shall perform this work,' for they two are about to perform this work. 6.6.2. [6]

"Strengthen yourself, O divine Earth, for our well-being!"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*). "Thou art the magical power (*māyā*) of the Asuras, fashioned by *svadhā*.
Breath indeed is the *asu*; this is its magical power fashioned by *svadhā*. "May this be pleasing to the gods."

"O thou who art to be invoked with oblations"—by this he refers to those very oblations which he is about to offer into this fire; and furthermore, "as an inviolable one, do thou rise up in this sacrifice"—he says this so that she may rise up in this sacrifice uninjured and unharmed. 6.6.2. [7]
He chooses it with two verses;

the sacrificer has two feet, and Agni is the sacrificer: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus chooses it—with both a *gāyatrī* and a *triṣṭubh*; the *gāyatrī* is breath, and the *triṣṭubh* is the self.

The Triṣṭubh is indeed as much as the animal is—namely, as much as its vital breath and its body; thus, by means of that which is as much as the animal, he thereby chooses it. Moreover, the Gāyatrī belongs to Agni and the Triṣṭubh to Indra, and Agni is of the nature of Indra and Agni; therefore, it is as much as Agni is, and as much as his measure is.
By that much he thus consecrates her. Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods; Agni belongs to all the deities.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus consecrates her. There are seven steps for those two;
the fire-altar consists of seven layers, there are seven seasons in the year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus consecrates her.
At that time, it becomes thus:
6.6.2.[8] When the fire heats her, then the flame mounts her. The fire-pan is indeed a woman, and the fire is a man; therefore, when the man—
He heats the woman, and then he places seed in her.
Now, some, if the flame has risen for a long time, throw down only embers, thinking, "This fire is both [the fire and the woman]. One should not do so;
for an animal is born possessed of bones, yet they do not deposit the seed into it as something already possessing bones from the very beginning.
Verily, they place seed therein; for that which is the flame is boneless. Therefore, one should mount it by means of the flame alone.
When he mounts it by means of the flame, he then places a fuel-stick upon it; for he thus bestows seed upon it. This [is the seed]. 6.6.2. [10]
In that semen, he places this generation.
It should be made of wood from a *kārmuka* tree.
Both the gods and the asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another; those gods made Agni their vanguard.

Having made an assault upon the Asuras with that [firebrand], the Asuras cut off the tip of it as it was being held up; it settled upon this earth and became the *kṛmuka* tree. Therefore, it has a sweet sap, for it is from that [sap]; therefore, it is red, for it is a flame. This *kṛmuka* is indeed Agni; he thus bestows the origin of Agni upon this [sacrificer]. 6.6.2. [12]
It is a span in measure.
For Viṣṇu, as an embryo, is a span in measure; he thus bestows upon him a growth commensurate with his own self. 6.6.2 [13]
It is placed in ghee. Ghee was the amnion of that womb from which Agni was emitted;
therefore it blazes up again, for this is his very self; therefore it has no ash.
"Then the self indeed enters the self, or rather it does not; [for] he destroys neither the caul nor the embryo, because of non-violence.
For from the caul one who is being born is born; may he be born from the caul as one being born. 6.6.2. He establishes that [fire].

"Wood-eating, with clarified butter as his draught"—this means "wood-consuming, with clarified butter as his food. "The ancient, desirable Hotṛ"—this means "the eternal, desirable Hotṛ. "The wonderful son of strength"—strength indeed is *sahas*;
thus, "the wonderful son of strength. Standing, he offers with the utterance of *svāhā*; the significance of this is explained above. 6.6.2. [15]

Verily, the fire-pan (ukhā) is the self; the muñja grass is the womb, the hemp is the chorion, the ghee is the amnion, and the fuel-stick is the embryo. The fire-pan is on the outside. 6.6.2. [16] It is external.
The muñja grass is outside, for the self is inside; the womb is outside, while the muñja grass is inside;
the hemp is outside, for the womb is inside; the afterbirth is outside, while the hemp is inside;
the ghee is inside, for the afterbirth is outside; the caul is outside, while the ghee is inside; the fuel-stick is inside, for it is outside.
The embryo is indeed within the womb; from these [elements] he is born when being born, and it is from them that he thus causes him to be born. 6.6.3.
[1] Then he places a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
That first oblation which Prajāpati offered—having offered it, where...

Then the *vikaṅkata* was rubbed; it became this first oblation, namely the *vikaṅkata*. He offers that to him at this point; by that he gratifies him [with the verse]: "From the far distance, come hither toward the nearer ones, to where I am; protect me! As the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*). 6.6.3. [2]
Then he places a branch of the Udumbara tree.
The gods and the Asuras, both offspring of Prajāpati, were contending;
all the trees of the forest went over to the Asuras, but the Udumbara alone did not desert the gods. Having conquered the Asuras, those gods—
They took away the sap from the trees.
They said, "Come now! Whatever vital energy and sap is in these trees, let us place it in the udumbara tree;
if they should depart, they will depart exhausted, like a milked-out cow or an ox that has finished its load."
Now, whatever strength and sap was in those trees, they placed it in the Udumbara;
therefore, by means of that strength, it ripens in rivalry with all the trees, which is why it is always moist and always milky.
Thus, the Udumbara is all this food—namely, all the trees—and so he [the sacrificer] is thereby provided with all this food.
"He gratifies with all the lords of the forest; he kindles [the fire] with the verse, 'From the furthest distance...'"—this means "from whatever is the furthest distance.
"'O you whose horses are ruddy, come hither!'"—this refers to Rohita.
"O Agni, thy horse, born of the soil, dear to many"—this means "belonging to cattle, dear to many. "O Agni, do thou overcome the adversaries"—this means "O Agni, do thou overcome all evils. 6.6.3.
[5] Then he places a piece cut by an axe.

When this [fire] is piled, it is born for all food; indeed, that which is not cut by an axe is one kind of food, and with that he gratifies him. "O Agni, whatever logs we lay upon you, may all that be ghee for you; enjoy that, O youngest one!"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its fulfillment.
That which is cut by an axe other than that [first one] is his kinsman; he makes that palatable for him and, having made it food for him, presents it to him.
Then he places the lower fire-stick.

He is born when he is piled; he is born for all kinds of food. This indeed is one kind of food, namely that which lies below; with that he gratifies him. "What the upajihvikā eats, what the ant crawls over"—for either the upajihvikā eats it or the ant crawls over it—"let all that be ghee for you."
"Enjoy that, O youngest one"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its bond (*bandhu*). Whatever food is placed below, that he makes palatable for him;
having made it food for him, he covers it over.
Now, these subsequent [spoons] are made of *palāśa* wood.
The Palāśa tree is indeed Brahman; he thus kindles him with Brahman.
Furthermore, as to why they are made of Palāśa wood: the Palāśa is Soma, and the oblation of Soma is the highest oblation; he thus offers that to him and thereby gratifies him. 6.6.3 [8]

"Bringing [offerings] day after day without ceasing"—this means bringing [them] day after day without becoming intoxicated. "Like fodder for a standing horse"—this means like fodder for a horse that stands [at its stall]. "Rejoicing with wealth and nourishment"—[so it is said].
"Rejoicing with wealth, with nourishment, and with food"— this [verse], "O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not come to harm," he says so that his neighbor may not suffer harm, just as he intends.
"When the fire is kindled on the navel of the earth"— [so he says].
"This is indeed the navel of the earth, where this [fire] is kindled here.
"For great abundance of wealth we call," he says; that is, "for wealth and for great abundance we call.
"The delight of refreshment (*irammada*)," he says, for he is intoxicated by refreshment (*ira*); "the one of great praise (*bṛhaduktha*)," he says, for he is indeed the one of great praise.

"Worshipful" means "worthy of sacrifice. "The conqueror Agni, the overcomer in battles"—for Agni is indeed a conqueror and an overcomer of armies. Those armies which are rushing forward... 6.6.3 [10]... [which are] attacking.
With your two fangs, [O Agni], crush those who are plunderers among the people, those who act as plunderers;
whoever acts with hostility toward us, and whatever person hates us, whoever reviles us and seeks to harm us—reduce all of them to ashes! 6.6.3. [11]

The gods, indeed, having made that food which someone hates and that which he himself hates into this [oblation], placed it within him; they gratified him with it, and it became his food. It burned away the evil of the gods.
In the same way, the sacrificer, having made food for both him who hates him and him whom he hates, places it [within him];
by this he gratifies him, and food indeed becomes his; he burns away the evil of the sacrificer.
He lays down these eleven [bricks].
For one who is neither a Kṣatriya nor a domestic priest, eleven [sacrificial cakes] are indeed incomplete;
for he who is neither a Kṣatriya nor a domestic priest is incomplete.
For a Kṣatriya or a domestic priest, there are twelve.
All that is indeed the twelve;
all that is the kṣatriya or the domestic priest.
He establishes [the fires] for the domestic priest.

"Sharpened is my sacred word (*brahman*), sharpened is my heroism and strength; sharpened is the victorious sovereignty (*kṣatra*) of him for whom I am the domestic priest. Thus he sharpens both his *brahman* and his *kṣatra*. 6.6.3. [15] Now, for the Kṣatriya:
"I have raised up their arms, I have raised up their luster and their strength;
with my sacred word (*brahman*), I destroy the enemies and I raise up my own people"—thus he says.

Just as one would indeed destroy the enemies and raise up his own people, so does he say this. Or rather, he should place both of these [formulas] together, for this fire is indeed the sacred word (*brahman*).
And the *kṣatra*; thus he kindles this very Agni with both of these—by means of the *brahman* and by means of the *kṣatra*.
These amount to thirteen.
Thirteen months are a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food does he thus gratify him.
They are a span long.
Viṣṇu, the embryo, is indeed the size of a span; this food is measured by his own self. Thus, he gratifies him with food that is commensurate with his own self.
For that food which is commensurate with one's self protects it and does not harm it; that which is more harms it, and that which is less does not [suffice].

Standing upon that [altar], he places the fuel; the significance of this has been explained above. This seed that was poured out is indeed this Agni. If he were to place pieces of wood into it without the utterance of *svāhā*, he would injure him.
Since they are *samidhs* (kindling-sticks), they are not offerings; but in that they are with the utterance of *svāhā*, they are food—for *svāhā* is indeed food—and thus it is so.
It does not harm him. 6.6.4.
[1] Then, having stepped with the Viṣṇu-strides and worshipped with the Vātsapra hymn, when the sun has set, [he should throw] only the ashes...

First he draws it out; for he gratifies him with this food and these kindling-sticks. Of that food which has been eaten, this impurity settles down as ashes; by means of those ashes, he thus separates him from it. When his impurity has been struck away, he releases his speech.
