Having released his speech, he places a kindling-stick on the fire for the sake of the night.

In this way he gratifies him with food, [with the verse]: "Bringing [fuel] night after night without ceasing. Its significance has been explained. For the night, he invokes this safety and well-being; whatever he adds to the fire during the night, he thereby adds for him as an act of offering. 6.6.4. [2]

Then, when the sun has risen in the morning, he first throws out the ashes. For with this food and with this fuel-stick he gratifies him; and that evil which belongs to the food he consumed during the night—that is what [the ashes represent].

The ashes settle; therefore, he turns him away from that. Upon that which is free from evil, he releases his speech. Having released his speech, he places a kindling-stick on the fire; verily, he thus gratifies him with food for the day. "Bringing it daily without fail,"—the significance of this has been explained. Verily, he invokes for himself this security and well-being for the day. And whatever else follows from this...
"He thus makes amends for it; verily, he makes amends for that which was caused by the oblation.
Day and night, as they revolve, reach the year; the year is this entire universe.
By means of the day, he invokes for him this security and well-being."
Now, when they hand over the fast-food (vrata) to him, he then anoints a fuel-stick (samidh) in the fast-food and places it on the fire; however,
some say that one should not anoint it in the fast-food, for one should offer it as a libation (āhuti), since it is improper for one who is consecrated (dīkṣita) to offer a libation.
"One should offer," [it is said]. 6.6.4.
[5] He should indeed anoint it downwards.
For that [sacrificial cake] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self. If he were not to anoint it downwards, he would not [unite] with that [divine self].

One should gratify the divine self; now, when he anoints [the fuel-stick], in that way he gratifies this divine self. Since it is a fuel-stick, it is not an oblation; and since it is anointed in the vow, it is food—for the vow is indeed food. Having placed the fuel-stick on the fire, he then undertakes the vow.

This [fire] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods were first, and then humans. Therefore, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he then undertakes the vow, saying: "O Lord of Food, give us food! (6.6.4).

"O Lord of food, give us food"—this means "of that which is free from disease and full of vigor," that is, "of that which is free from hunger and full of vigor. "Further further the giver"—the giver is indeed the sacrificer; thus he says, "further the sacrificer.
"Bestow strength upon the two-footed and the four-footed"—he thereby invokes a blessing. As for what...
Regarding the expiation for a cracked [fire-pan], it is stated in the subsequent explanatory section (6.6.4):
"If this fire-pan should break, one should pour this [fire] into another unbroken pot that has a wide opening while reciting [the verse]: 'O Agni, do not abandon us... (RV 1.189.2).
This fire-pan which breaks is indeed uninjured; this deity is uninjured, [thinking], "May I support this uninjured one within myself while being uninjured.
Thereupon, he throws a potsherd from the pan into the fire beforehand; thus, indeed, it does not fall away from its womb.
Then, having brought clay...

Having ground both the fire-pan (ukhā) and the secondary pan (upaśayā), he mixes them and fashions the fire-pan according to this same procedure; they bring [the materials] forward without a formal sacrificial formula (yajus), and having baked it silently, he pours [the contents] around. In that case, the ritual action itself is the expiation. Then, having placed that potsherd back into the fire-pan, and having ground both the fire-pan and the secondary pan, he mixes them together.

He places [the fire] for the sake of expiations (prāyaścitti). 6.6.4. Now, if this fire in the fire-pan (ukhya) should go out, it goes back indeed to the Gārhapatya, for from the Gārhapatya it [originated].

It has been brought [to the fire]. Having drawn it out from the *gārhapatya* fire facing eastward and having kindled it, he should place the fire-pan (*ukhā*) upon it according to this same procedure. Without reciting a sacrificial formula, he should carry it forward silently. When the fire ascends into it, he then performs the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitti*).

Verily, he establishes this [fire] for the sake of all his desires; whatever of his desires is cut off here when the fire goes out, that he now makes continuous and joins together. He performs both expiations:
the expiation for the sacrifice and the expiation for the fire. The former is for the sacrifice, and then for the fire; the [explanation] of that has been stated.

[The section on] the relative, 6.6.4.[12]: Having taken a portion of the clarified butter with the *samidh* stick while seated, he offers the oblation with the words, "To Viśvakarman, svāhā! and then, having stood up.
He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the verse: "May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle thee again; may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, [kindle thee] with sacrifices.
This means, "May these deities kindle thee again. "With ghee, do thou increase thy body;
may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled"—by this he says, "Do thou increase with ghee," for those [desires] for which...
"The sacrificer has established you for the sake of desires; may all these of his become true"—this is what he means.
Now, if the Gārhapatya fire should go out, it has indeed gone into the two kindling woods (araṇī), for it was brought from the two kindling woods.
Having churned him out from the two kindling sticks (*araṇi*) and enkindled him, he performs the expiation. 6.6.4.
[14] Now, if the *āhavanīya* fire should go out while the Soma-pressing is underway, it goes back to the *gārhapatya*, for it originated from the *gārhapatya*.
It has been brought; having fetched it from the *gārhapatya* fire itself toward the east by means of a mirror and having kindled it, he performs the expiation.
Whatever sacrifice (*adhvara*) might be in progress at that time, he should perform the expiation for that sacrifice;
the expiation for the fire is the same. 6.6.4. [15]
Now, if the Āgnīdhrīya fire should go out,
it goes back to the Gārhapatya, for it was brought from the Gārhapatya;
having carried it from the Gārhapatya itself eastward along the north side of the Sadas and having kindled it, one should perform the expiation.
Now, if the *gārhapatya* fire should go out, its significance has already been explained.
Having fastened on a gold plate (*rukma*), he carries it;
for the gold plate is truth, and truth indeed is able to sustain him.
By means of truth the gods bore him; by means of truth alone he now bears him. 6.7.1.
[2] Now, that which is truth is yonder sun; it is golden, for gold is light and this one is light.

Gold is immortal; this [mirror] is circular, for it is circular. It has twenty-one knobs, for it is the twenty-first. It bears the knobs on its outer side, for the knobs are its rays, and its rays are indeed on the outside. 6.7.1. [3]
And furthermore, as to why he carries the gold plate after having fastened it on:
yonder sun is indeed this gold plate; for no mere human is able to approach this Agni in his human form; rather, by means of this very form, he carries that [divine] form. 6.7.1. [4]
Moreover, as to why he carries the gold plate after fastening it on:
this [gold plate] is indeed seed that has been sprinkled; this Agni is brilliance and vigor, and the gold plate is brilliance and vigor;
thus he places brilliance and vigor into that seed. 6.7.1. [5]
As for the fact that he wears the gold plate after fastening it on:
the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this one here"; therefore...
They made that very sun their protector from this side; for yonder sun is indeed this *rukma*.
In the same way, he now makes him his protector from this side. It is strung upon a black antelope skin.
The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; the sacrifice is indeed able to sustain this [body].

By means of the sacrifice the gods carried it away; by means of the sacrifice he now carries it. It is on the hairy side; for the hairs are the meters, and the meters are indeed able to sustain this. By means of the meters the gods [carried it].
Verily, by means of the *chandases* (metres), he thus carries him. 6.7.1.
[7] It is woven through with white and black threads;
for these are the forms of *ṛc* and *sāman*, and it is indeed *ṛc* and *sāman*.
"You ought to restrain this. The gods bore him with the *ṛk* and the *sāman*;
verily, by means of the *ṛk* and the *sāman*, he now bears him. The linen cord for the gold plate (*rukma*) is threefold; its significance has been explained.
He wears it above the navel.
This sun, indeed, is this gold plate (rukma), and it is above the navel.
For what reason it is above the navel:
below the navel is seed, and Prajāpati is brilliance and vigor; [he places it there] so that his seed shall not...
"May the gold plate burn forth procreation, brilliance, and vigor for thee.
And as to why it is above the navel:
that part of the animal which is above the navel is indeed more pure and more closely connected with the vital essence (*purīṣa*).
That which is below the navel is the most sacrificially pure part of the animal; with that he thus carries him.
And as for what is above the navel:
that which is above the navel is the immortal part of the vital breath.

Now, that which is mortal rises up with the vital breaths; it does not go beyond the navel. That which is the immortal element of the vital breath, with that he now unites him; by means of that, he thus supports him. 6.7.1.
Then he supports him on the throne-seat.

This indeed is the seat (āsandi), for upon it all this is seated; this indeed is fit to support him. With this the gods carried him; with this he now carries him. It is made of Udumbara wood. 6.7.1. [13] It is made of Udumbara wood.

The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; he thus supports him with strength and sap. Moreover, the Udumbara is all these trees; all these trees are worthy of carrying him. With all these trees the gods carried him; with all these trees he thus carries him. 6.7.1 [14]
It is one span high;

for Viṣṇu, the embryo, is indeed one span, and this is the womb; thus he makes the womb commensurate with the embryo. It is one cubit wide across; for the cubit is the arm, and by means of the arm [one reaches].
Vigor is exerted; it becomes commensurate with that vigor, for vigor is indeed capable of restraining this [chariot].
By means of vigor the gods carried it; by means of vigor he carries it now.
Its feet have four corners.
The verses to be recited have four corners; for there are indeed four quarters, and it is the quarters that are able to sustain him.

By means of the quarters the gods carried him; by means of the quarters he thus carries him. It is woven with cords of muñja grass, triple-stranded; the significance of that has been explained. It is smeared with clay; the significance of that also has been explained. And furthermore—
[It is] so that there may be no excessive burning. 6.7.1.[16] Now he carries it by means of a sling.
These worlds, indeed, are this Agni; the quarters are the sling, for these worlds are supported by the quarters.
They are able to stand firm; because they are able to stand, he carries him (the fire) by means of the quarters.
It is six spans high, for there are six quarters. It is made of muñja grass and is threefold; the significance of that has been explained. It is smeared with clay;
the significance of that also has been explained, and furthermore, it is to prevent excessive burning.

Water is its foundation, for these worlds are founded upon water; the sun is the attachment, for these worlds are attached to the sun by means of the quarters. He who knows this thus—by this very form he bears that form. 6.7.1. [18]
Moreover, as to why he carries him by means of a sling:

this Agni is the year, and the sling is the seasons; for by means of the seasons the year is able to stand firm, and because it is able [to do so], it is called a "sling" (śikya); thus, by means of the seasons, he thereby carries him.
It consists of six *udya* measures; there are six seasons. Its foundation is day and night, for upon day and night this year and the moon are established.

For this year is attached to the moon by means of the seasons. He who knows this thus bears this form by means of that very form. Indeed, for him who knows this, this [year] becomes one maintained for a year; but for him who does not know this, it remains merely worshipped for a year. This is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam). 6.7.1. [20]
Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātman*):

the self itself is the fire; the breaths are the sling-strap (*śikya*), for by means of the breaths this self is able to stand; and because it is able [to stand], therefore it is the sling-strap. By means of the breaths he thus supports it. It has six suspension-ropes (*udyāma*), for there are six...
The vital breaths (prāṇas) [are its support]. Its very mind is its foundation; for this self is established in the mind, which is attached to food in food.
For this self is joined with the vital breaths; he who knows this thus, by means of this very form, bears that form. 6.7.1.
[22] Now, he bears it with a fire-pan (*ukhā*).
These worlds, indeed, are the fire-pan; these worlds, indeed, bear him.
The gods were able to carry him by means of these worlds; verily, by means of these very worlds he now carries him.
As for why it is called an *ukhā*:
the gods, by means of this—
By means of this rite, they dug out these worlds with a spade (*utkha*). Because they dug them out (*udakhanan*), it is called "utkhītkhā" cryptically;
for the gods love the cryptic.
Now, "ukhā" consists of two syllables.

The sacrificer has two feet; the sacrificer is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he thus supports him. That [pot] is a *kumbhī*, that is a *sthālī*. That makes six;
there are six seasons, and the year consists of six seasons. The year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. 6.7.1. [25]
Then he encloses it with two *iṇḍva*-sticks.
Yonder sun is indeed this fire; day and night are the two *iṇḍva*-sticks.
He thus encloses yonder sun with day and night; therefore, it is enclosed by day and night. 6.7.1 [26]
Moreover, as to why he encloses it with two clods of earth:
yonder sun is this Agni, and these worlds are the two clods;
he thus encloses yonder sun with these two worlds, and therefore it is encompassed by these two worlds.
They are taken up and become circular; these two worlds are indeed circular. They are made of muñja grass and are threefold;
the significance of that has been explained. They are smeared with clay; the significance of that has also been explained, and furthermore, it is to prevent excessive burning.
Now, therefore, regarding the correspondence.
The stool, the pan, the sling, the cord for the gold plate, the fire, and the gold plate—these are six.

The seasons are six, and the year is [composed of] six; Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become. These [objects] are eight; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables; Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. As great as Agni is, as great as is his...
First, that constitutes the measure:
6.7.1.[28]. Now, the complete prosperity [consists of]:
four feet, four sections to be recited, a sling, and the loop for the gold plate—whatever else there may be.
And there is the cord, the sling, and following that the fire-pan, the fire, and the gold ornament—these make thirteen. Thirteen months are a year;
the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does this become.
Standing, he fastens it on.
Yonder sun, indeed, is this gold plate. For yonder sun stands, as it were;
and standing, one is indeed more powerful. Standing facing north-east—its significance has been explained.
"The shining gold plate has shone forth widely."

"For this gold plate (rukma), being seen, flashes across the wide earth with an unendurable life-span, shining for the sake of glory"— for its life-span is indeed difficult to die, and it shines for the sake of glory. "'Agni became immortal through his vital powers' (vayobhiḥ)"— for he indeed became immortal through all his vital powers when the sky gave birth to him.
"Verily, the sky begat him with good seed"—for she is indeed one with good seed whose seed he is. 6.7.2.
[3] Then he encloses him with two fingers, saying, "Night and Dawn, like-minded though diverse in form"—verily, these are day and night.

"Night and Dawn, of one mind yet different forms, moving together, suckle the one infant"—whatever indeed there is of day and night, by that they suckle this very one together. "The radiant gem shines between heaven and earth"—carrying [the fire], he mutters this sacrificial formula; for these two, heaven and earth, are heaven and earth, and it is between them that this shines.
Therefore, he mutters this supporting *yajus*: "The gods, the givers of wealth, supported Agni. Having grasped it, he sets it down.
The gods who are the givers of wealth are indeed the vital breaths; they supported him thus at the very beginning, and by means of them, he now supports him.
Then he fastens the sling-loop.
"The Sage assumes all forms"—the Sage is indeed yonder Āditya;

"he has sent forth all forms, the sling"—as he rises, he sends forth what is auspicious for bipeds and quadrupeds. "Savitar, the most excellent, has looked upon the vault of heaven"—the vault of heaven is indeed the world of heaven.
"Looking back upon the ascent of heaven, he shines following the departure of the Dawn"— for indeed, the Dawn first dawns,
and shining after her dawning, he rises up. Then, from this point on, he fashions him with the *vikṛti* (the modification).
"This very semen, once emitted, undergoes transformation; therefore, the semen emitted in the female organ undergoes transformation.
"You are the fair-winged Garuḍa."
Vīrya indeed is Suparṇa Garutman; he thus bestows vīrya upon him. "The Trivṛt is thy head," he says; he makes the Trivṛt stoma his head.
"The Gāyatra is the eye," he says; he makes the Gāyatra the eye. "The Bṛhat and Rathantara are the wings," he says.

He makes the Bṛhat and Rathantara the two wings; "the Stoma is the self," thus he makes the Stoma the self. "The Pañcaviṃśa [Stoma] and the metres are the limbs"—for the metres are indeed its limbs. "The Yajus-formulas are its name"—that which they call it "Agni" is its name consisting of the Yajus-formulas. "The Vāmadevya Sāman is your body"—the body is indeed the self; it is your self.
"The body is the Vāmadevya"—this refers to the Yajñāyajñīya; "the tail is the Yajñāyajñīya"—thus he makes the Yajñāyajñīya the tail.
"The Dhiṣṇya hearths are the hooves"—for by means of the Dhiṣṇyas, this [Agni] is established in this world. "Thou art a well-winged Garuḍa;
go to heaven, fly to the light!"—having thus made him a well-winged Garuḍa, he says: "Go to the gods, to the heavenly world."

He causes it to fall. Indeed, at this point he fashions it with wings and a tail. For whatever kind of seed is fashioned in the womb, such is what is born; since he fashions it here with wings and a tail, therefore it [is so] there in the other world.
It is born with wings and a tail.

6.7.2.[8] Regarding this, some, having consecrated it with this modified formula (*vikṛti*), pile another layer (*citi*): either a *droṇacit*, or a *rathacakracit*, or a *kaṅkacit*, or a *praugacit*, or one with *prauga*s on both sides, or one with leveled earth (*samuhyapurīṣa*). One should not do so.
One should construct it so that it has wings and a tail; one should cut out the interior in such a manner.
Therefore, one should pile it as the Suparṇaciti (the eagle-pile) with this modification. 6.7.2.
[9] One should perform it with this modification.
From here upwards he holds it forward; for yonder sun is this Agni, and thus he places yonder sun from here upwards and forward.
Therefore yonder sun is placed from here upwards and forward. He holds it beyond the reach of his arms, for he is indeed beyond the reach of our arms from here. Then he lowers it.
Having brought it down, he holds it above the navel; the significance of this has been explained. 6.7.2.
[10] Then he strides the Viṣṇu-strides. For the gods, having become Viṣṇu, strode across these worlds.

Because Viṣṇu, having become [the sacrifice], strode across [these worlds], therefore they are called the Viṣṇu-strides; in the very same way, the sacrificer, having become Viṣṇu, strides across these worlds.
That which is Viṣṇu is the sacrifice.
That sacrifice which is there is this very one; it is this fire here in the fire-pan.
Having made themselves this very self, the gods stepped forth to these worlds. In the same way, the sacrificer, having made himself this very self, steps forth to these worlds. 6.7.2. [12]

Standing facing north-east—Prajāpati, indeed, standing facing north-east, created offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides; in the very same way, the sacrificer, standing facing north-east, creates offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides. 6.7.2. [13]
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he says;

for having become Viṣṇu, he strides. "Slaying the rivals," he says; for here he slays his rivals. "Mount the Gāyatrī metre," he says; for he mounts the Gāyatrī metre. "Stride along the earth," he says.
He strides along the earth; he strikes out, he steps forth, and he lifts his foot upward; for he rises upward, he takes hold of Agni.
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," for having become Viṣṇu, he strides; "the slayer of the adversary," for here he slays the adversaries.

"He ascends to the *traiṣṭubha* metre"—he indeed ascends to the *traiṣṭubha* metre. "Stride along the intermediate space"—he strides along the intermediate space; he strikes down one foot as he steps forward, lifting the fire upward, for he ascends upward. 6.7.2. [15]
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu.
For having become Viṣṇu, he strides; "to slay those who act as enemies"—here he indeed slays those who act as enemies.
"Mount the Jāgata metre"—he mounts the Jāgata metre. "Stride along after heaven"—along after heaven.
"He strides, he strikes, he steps; he lifts the fire upward, for he indeed ascends.
[With the words] "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," for having become Viṣṇu, he strides; "slaying those who act as enemies," for here he slays those who act as enemies.

"May he slay the *anuṣṭubh* metre; ascend to the *anuṣṭubh* metre," with these words he ascends to the *anuṣṭubh* metre. "Stride along the quarters," with these words he gazes toward all the quarters. He does not set down his foot, thinking, "Lest I utterly destroy these worlds. He raises the fire only upwards, for he is ascending. 6.7.3. [1]
Then he takes it up with the words, "Now him.
For the gods indeed desired, "May we become Parjanya in form";
by means of this self, they became Parjanya in form. In the same way, the sacrificer, by means of this self, becomes Parjanya.
The form is:
"Agni has cried out, like the thundering sky," for Parjanya,
as it were, cries out while thundering over the earth.
"Licking repeatedly, he anoints the plants"—the earth is indeed Parjanya; licking repeatedly, he anoints the plants.

"As soon as born, kindled, he has looked abroad"—as soon as he is born, he indeed makes all this visible. "He shines between the two worlds with his light"—these two worlds are indeed heaven and earth; he shines between them with his light.
He holds it above his head, for Parjanya is indeed above the arms.
Then he brings it down;
for whatever essence there is in this world, whatever provides sustenance—with that he thus ascends together.

Agni ascends these worlds; Agni is indeed the essence (*rasa*) in this world, the means of subsistence. If it were only to ascend, there would be neither essence nor means of subsistence in this world. But when he descends again, he places that very essence and means of subsistence back into this world. 6.7.3 [4]
Moreover, as to why he descends again:

when he ascends from here upwards to these worlds, that ascent is, as it were, directed away; but this [earth] is indeed the firm foundation. If it were only so much, the sacrificer would surely fall away from this world. Therefore...
In that he descends thus, he approaches this very foundation; he establishes himself upon this very foundation. 6.7.3.
[5] That he descends in this manner.
Verily, this [sacrifice] wins these worlds from here upwards. That victory is, as it were, a one-sided victory;
for indeed, others settle upon what has been won by him who wins only in one direction. But he who wins in both ways, for him there is freedom of movement in that regard.
Now, when he descends, he thereby conquers these very worlds—both those above here and those below.
"O Agni, you who turn back! Turn back toward me! O Agni Aṅgiras, with vigor and with wealth!"—with this [he prays], "Do not abandon me."
"Return from all [sides]," he says; thus he descends four times. For four times he ascends upwards;
as many times as he ascends upwards, so many times does he descend. Having brought it down, he holds it above the navel; the significance of this has been explained. 6.7.3. [7]
Then he addresses it with the mantra:

"Agni is life; verily, he thus places life within himself. With the words, "I have brought thee hither," for they indeed bring him hither; with the words, "Thou hast entered within," he thus places life within himself.

"Stand firm, immovable"—he thus places this firm life-span within his own self. "May all the subjects desire you"—the subjects are indeed food; he means, "may all food desire you. "May the kingdom not fall away from you"—the kingdom is indeed prosperity; he means, "may prosperity not fall away from you. 6.7.3 [8]
Then he unfastens both the sling-rope and the gold-plate rope.
The rope belongs to Varuṇa; thus he is released from Varuṇa’s noose by means of a verse addressed to Varuṇa, that is, by his own self and by his own deity.

"He is released from Varuṇa’s noose with [the verse]: 'O Varuṇa, loosen the highest noose from us, the lowest, and the middle one. As the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*). Then [he says]: 'O Āditya, may we be sinless (*anāgasaḥ*) in your service for the sake of Aditi.
Aditi is indeed this earth; thus he means, 'May we be sinless toward you and toward her.'"
Then he holds it up with the words, "athainaṃ" (then him).
For having fashioned it there [in the fire], he now holds it up from here upwards and towards the east.

He holds it up with the words, "taṃ tataḥ" (him from there). If it were only as much as that, it would surely have come to rest right there; but because he says "atha yadenaṃ" (now him), [he brings it forward].
"Therefore he grasps [it], saying: 'Having gone thus, he comes back again.
(6.7.3) "Great and lofty, he has stood at the head of the dawns," for indeed, great and lofty, he stands at the head of the dawns.
"He has come forth from darkness with light"—for indeed, this Agni comes forth from the darkness of night with the light of day;
"Agni, fair-limbed with radiant luster"—for this Agni is indeed fair-limbed with radiant luster;
"As soon as born, he has filled all dwellings"—for these worlds are indeed all the dwellings, and as soon as he is born, he fills them beyond the reach of the arm.
He raises it above his head; for this [sacrifice] goes from here upwards. Then he brings it down; he thereby returns toward this very foundation and establishes himself upon this very foundation.
With the *jagatī* [verse], for these worlds are the *jagatī*; from there he extends downwards across these worlds. 6.7.3. [11]
"The swan dwelling in purity"—that swan dwelling in purity is indeed yonder sun; "the Vasu dwelling in the intermediate space"—the Vasu dwelling in the intermediate space is indeed Vāyu;
"the Hotṛ dwelling at the altar"—the Hotṛ dwelling at the altar is indeed Agni; "the guest"—for he is the guest of all.
"He is the guest of beings, seated in the dwelling"—this means "seated in the uneven. "Seated among men" (*nṛṣat*): the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed "seated among men," for men are *nara*s;
thus he refers to that fire which is the vital breath among men. "Seated in the choice" (*varasat*): for he is seated in all choice things.
"Seated in the cosmic order" (*ṛtasat*): this means "seated in truth. "Seated in the sky" (*vyomasat*): for he is seated in all spaces. He is born from the waters.

"Born of the cow" (gojā) means "born of the waters" (abjā), for he is indeed born of the cow; "born of the seasons" (ṛtajā) means "born of truth" (satyajā); "born of the rock" (adrijā) means he is indeed born of the rock; "the Right" (ṛtam) means "the Truth" (satyam).
He places [the stone] with the word "Great" (bṛhat), for he is great; having thus made him what he is, he places him. With two syllables. VI.7.3. [12]
The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just that much he thus establishes him.
Then he stands in worship before him.
For indeed, it is as if this [sacrifice] becomes light for him when he strides through these worlds with "this" and "that"; he thus makes amends to it for the sake of non-injury.
And furthermore, as to why he stands in attendance.

The gods were indeed afraid of this, thinking, "Lest he should destroy these worlds of ours from their very vicinity. They thus appeased him for these worlds; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now appeases him for these worlds. 6.7.3. [15]

"Sit down on the lap of this mother; O Agni, with your splendor, becoming auspicious for me, O Agni, sit down—be you auspicious! By saying "auspicious, auspicious," he thus pacifies him for the sake of non-injury; and so indeed does he [become].
And he does not harm these worlds with his end.
He worships with three [verses].
These worlds are three; moreover, Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—
By that much alone he makes amends for him; moreover, by that much he pacifies him for these worlds.
Then he worships with the Vātsapra hymn.
For having created offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati [performed this] for them.
Just as he [the creator] bestowed long life by means of the Vātsapra hymn, so too does the sacrificer, having created offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides,
bestow long life upon them by means of the Vātsapra. This, indeed, is the Dākṣāyaṇa-hand.

Or rather, regarding that Vātsapra: if one should desire of a newborn child, "May he attain a full lifespan," one should touch him with the Vātsapra; this bestows longevity upon him as soon as he is born, and thus he attains a full lifespan. Furthermore, if one should desire of him, "May he be vigorous," one should [touch] him with the Vikṛti.
One should consecrate him beforehand; thus he indeed becomes possessed of vigor. (6.7.4) "From heaven Agni was first born"—heaven is indeed breath, and from breath he [Agni] arises.

"First he was born from us; second, Jātavedas [was born] around [us]"—this refers to when they then produced him a second time in human form. "Third in the waters"—this refers to when they then produced him a third time from the waters.
"Nṛmaṇas, the unaging"—Prajāpati indeed is Nṛmaṇas and Agni is the unaging. "Kindling him, the well-disposed one praises him"—whoever [is such].
The one who knows kindles him; he, being well-disposed, brings him forth.
"O Agni, we know your three triads"—namely Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya; these indeed are his three triads that they know.

"Those abodes of yours are distributed in many places"—this refers to how they are distributed here in many ways. "I know your supreme name which is hidden in secret"—O youngest one (*yaviṣṭha*), this indeed is your supreme name hidden in secret; "I know that fountain from which you have come"—the fountain is indeed the waters, for he first came from the waters. "We honor you in the ocean with our praise."

"Within the waters"—Prajāpati is indeed *nṛmaṇas* (man-minded); "thee within the waters, O Prajāpati"—this is what it means. "The man-beholding one kindled thee in the udder of heaven, O Agni"—Prajāpati is indeed the man-beholding one, and the waters are the udder of heaven. "Thee standing in the third realm"—the sky is indeed the third realm; "in the lap of the waters the buffalo-bulls increased thee"—the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the buffalo-bulls; [they increased thee] in the sky.
"The vital breaths increased"—this is [the meaning].

These [verses] have a single explanation. They refer to this very [Agni]; they are *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*). Since they are addressed to Agni, therefore they belong to Agni. Furthermore—

In that it is a *triṣṭubh* and has eleven syllables, it is Indra; Agni belongs to Indra and Agni. By as much as is his measure, by just so much does he thus worship him. Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods, and Agni belongs to all the deities. By as much as is [his measure]... Furthermore, as to why there are the *viṣṇukrama* and the *vātsapra*.

By the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created offspring; by that much he thus worships him. By the Vātsapra, Prajāpati created this world; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Agni; by the Vātsapra, Vāyu; and by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the sky.

By means of the Vātsapra hymn, Prajāpati created the Āditya; by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, he created the quarters. By means of the Vātsapra hymn, Prajāpati created the moon; by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, he created what has been. By means of the Vātsapra hymn, Prajāpati created what will be;
by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, he created wealth. By means of the Vātsapra hymn, Prajāpati created the region; by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, he created the day.
By means of the Vātsapra hymn and the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the first fortnights;

by means of the Vātsapra hymn and the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the latter fortnights; by means of the Vātsapra hymn and the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the half-months; by means of the Vātsapra hymn and the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the months; by means of the Vātsapra hymn and the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the seasons; and by means of the Vātsapra hymn, [he created] the year.

In that there are the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra, by that he creates this entire universe. Furthermore, as to why there are the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra: by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati [attained] heaven.
He set out toward the world with the intention [of reaching it]; he saw this Vātsapra as the place of rest. With that he came to rest, so that there might be no burning.

For indeed, that which is yoked but not unyoked is burned up; in the very same way, the sacrificer proceeds toward the heavenly world by means of the Viṣṇu-strides and comes to rest with the Vātsapra. 6.7.4. [8]

Having indeed stepped out with the Viṣṇu-strides, he then immediately worships with the Vātsapra; it is just as if one were to set out on a journey and then immediately release [the horses]. It is according to the ordinance of the gods that men act; therefore, this is so even here.
The human village sets out at that very moment and then rests. Indeed, the Viṣṇu-strides are the day and night; the Vātsapra is the day and night;
[it is] indeed in the day and night.

Thus he goes for a day and a night; he becomes secure. Therefore, even here on earth, a human village, having gone for a day and a night, becomes secure for a day and a night. He indeed strides the Viṣṇu-strides for only half of the year.
He worships with the Vātsapra hymn for half [the year];

for the heavenly world is in the middle of the year. If he were to step forward less than half [the year], he would not reach that heavenly world; but if he steps beyond half [the year], he passes beyond that heavenly world.
Then, half of the world perishes through ignorance, while the other half proceeds and attains it; having reached the heavenly world, that [half] is released.
6.7.4.[11] Indeed, by means of those two, one undergoes a reversal.

Just as one might traverse a long road by means of a release, so too does he combine both the Viṣṇukrama and the Vātsapra, the former at the beginning and the latter at the end. For the Viṣṇukramas are the day and the Vātsapra is the night; indeed, Prajāpati combined these two when he was about to bring forth this entire universe.
Having brought them forth, he encloses them on both sides by means of day and night.

Regarding this, they say: "Since the Vishnu-strides are performed during the day and the Vatsapra during the night—both of these thus belong to the day and not to the night—how is it that they also come to be performed for him on the night? To this, [the answer is]: "When he is being consecrated, he [performs them] beforehand in the afternoon."

He combines both [the days] at night, for this [night] is the afternoon; then, about to join them together, he combines both in the forenoon, for this [forenoon] is the day. Thus, indeed, both are made into a day for him, and both into a night. 6.7.4. [13]

On the day when he is about to mix [the ashes], on that morning, after the sun has risen, he first scoops out the ashes; having scooped out the ashes, he releases his speech; having released his speech, he places a fuel-stick on the fire;
having placed the fuel-stick, he carries the ashes down into the water. Just as there is that carrying down of them, so too, having taken them up...
Having returned from the ashes and having placed [the ashes] back into the fire-pan (ukhā), he stands in worship; then he performs the expiatory rites (prāyaścitti).
If it should be the day for the Viṣṇu-strides, having performed the Viṣṇu-strides, he should stand in worship with the Vātsapra hymn; and if...

Having worshipped with the Vātsapra [hymn] and having performed the Viṣṇu-strides, one should perform the Vātsapra at the end, but not the Viṣṇu-strides at the end; for that would be as if, having set out, one did not release [the journey]. Now, as for why he performs the Vātsapra at the end: the Vātsapra is indeed a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). Just as...
One should establish and settle it; therefore, one should finally perform the *vātsapra* rite.
"One should carry Agni about," they say. The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, were contending with one another. 6.8.1. [1]

The gods moved about on a wagon, while the Asuras remained stationary. Moving about on a wagon, the gods perceived this ritual act; for it was while moving about on a wagon that the gods perceived this ritual act. Therefore, the sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) for the sacrificial cakes (*pauroḍāśa*) belong to the wagon, and [the formulas] for the fire belong to the wagon. 6.8.1. [2]

He who is carried about as a bridegroom goes to the gods by his action; indeed, a divine action is performed by him. But he who is not carried about as a bridegroom goes to the Asuras by his action; indeed, an Asuric action is performed by him. 6.8.1.3.
Regarding this, some say: "He has indeed been led away by himself; he departs with the Viṣṇu-strides and settles down with the Vātsapra.
One should not understand it thus; for that departure of his which consists of the Viṣṇu-strides is indeed a divine departure.
That which is the divine end is the Vātsapra; this human departure is that which departs as the human end, and that which comes to rest is the [human] end. 6.8.1.[4] This Agni is Prajāpati.
Both of these belong to Prajāpati: the gods and the humans. In that there are the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra hymn, he thereby prepares for him that which is his divine form;
and in that the cow is driven away, he thereby prepares for him that which is his human form. He...
Verily, he who, knowing this, undergoes the *vanīvāhya* rite, constructs this entire Prajāpati in his completeness;
therefore, one should indeed undergo the *vanīvāhya* rite.
On the day when he is about to set out...
On that day, having placed fuel on the fire from the north towards the east, he then places a kindling-stick upon it; for the gods, when he was about to go forth,
gratified him beforehand with food by means of this kindling-stick, and in the same way does this sacrificer now [gratify him] as he is about to go forth.
First, he gratifies him with food by means of this kindling-stick: "Worship Agni with the kindling-stick.
With the kindling-stick, [he worships] Agni.

"Pay homage"—this means "awaken the guest with clarified butter. "Offer the oblations in him"—this means "awaken the guest with clarified butter; offer the oblations in him. By saying "he has awakened," he indeed awakens him for protection. 6.8.1 [7]
Then he lifts it up with the verse:
"May all the gods, O Agni, lift thee up with their thoughts. For indeed, in the beginning, all the gods lifted him up with their thoughts; for such was their state at that time.

"The mind was indeed thus; him he now raises up with these layers (*citayaḥ*), for that is his mind at that time. "Be thou auspicious to us, O Vibhāvasu, of fair aspect"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its bond. He places it on the south side, facing north; the significance of this is as follows: having poured the Gārhapatya fire into a pot, he places another [fire] upon it, if...
He may desire to mount [the cart] or walk alongside it. Then he yokes the two oxen:
first the right one, then the left; thus it is among the gods, otherwise among men.

In whichever direction one intends to go, one should first set out toward the east; for the east is the direction of Agni, and thus one proceeds along one's own quarter. "Come forward, O Agni, full of light! [6.8.1.9]
"With auspicious flames, O Agni, come hither"—that is to say, "O Agni, come hither as one possessed of light with your auspicious, blazing flames.
"Shining with great beams, do not harm our offspring with your body"—that is to say, "with your great, blazing flames, do not harm our offspring through yourself. 6.8.1 [10]

Whenever the axle makes a sound, he should then mutter this sacrificial formula (*yajus*): "This speech of the axle is indeed asurya; he thereby appeases it and makes it belong to the gods. 6.8.1. [11]
Moreover, as for why he mutters this sacrificial formula (*yajus*):
whenever one lets out a sound while something has been placed upon an axle, that sound belongs to that very thing;
so when one lets out a sound while something has been placed upon the fire, that sound belongs to the fire itself. Thus, the gods [made it] belong to Agni alone.
They praised him and magnified him; in the same way, this [priest] now praises and magnifies him. "Agni has roared like the thundering sky"—the significance of this has already been explained. 6.8.1.
[12] Now, if he should release [the horse] before the night's stay.

It should be like fire on a wagon. Then, when he unyokes it for staying overnight, having placed the wagon facing eastward, he digs up the ground to the north and sprinkles it with water. Wherever he brings it down, he brings it down to the south, facing north; the significance of this has been explained. 6.8.1. [13]
Then he places a fuel-stick upon it;
for when he had gone forth, the gods gratified him from above with food by means of this fuel-stick.
In this very way, he gratifies him who has come here with food from above by means of this kindling-stick (samidh) with [the verse]:
"Far-famed is this Agni of Bharata.
Prajāpati is indeed Bharata, for he sustains all this.
"When he shines forth like the sun with great light"—this means "when he shines forth like the sun with great light.

"He who stood against Pūru in the battles"—Pūru was indeed a name for an *asura*-rakṣasa; against him Agni stood in the battles. "The divine guest has shone, auspicious as it were"—that is, the divine guest, shining, is auspicious as it were.
This [fire], being established, causes him to dwell there; for this is the dwelling of that which has been established. 6.8.1.[15] Now, therefore, follows the ritual correspondence (*sampad*):
he places a fuel-stick with the first [verse] and lifts it up with one [verse].
With one [verse] he goes forward; with one he consecrates [the fuel]; with five he lays on the kindling-stick. That makes five. The fire-altar consists of five layers;
there are five seasons in a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become. 6.8.2.1.
Now, therefore, regarding the consumption of ashes:
In the beginning, the gods scattered these ashes; they said, "If we were to fashion ourselves out of this while it remains just as it is, we would become mortal corpses."
"We shall not be rid of evil if we should miss [the fire]; that which is of Agni here will be outside of Agni.
Consider how we may perform this. They said, "Meditate!
By which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek how we may perform this. 6.8.2.2.

As they were reflecting, they saw this: "Let us carry it into the waters; for the waters are the foundation of all this. Having established it there where the foundation of all this is, whatever here belongs to Agni—"
"Let us generate it from these waters," he said; so they cast it into the waters. In the same way, this [priest] now casts it into the waters.
"O divine waters, receive this ash; make for it a pleasant and fragrant place," he says, for it has indeed been consumed.
This becomes exhausted; therefore, he says this: "Make this world most excellent for him;

let the progenies bow down to him. The progenies are indeed the waters, for from the waters all this is born. "With good wives"—for the waters have Agni as their good husband—"bear him in your lap like a mother her son," that is, just as a mother bears her son in her lap.
"One should indeed support him; thus he supports him.
(6.8.2.4) "O Agni, your seat is in the waters"—this means, "O Agni, your womb is in the waters"; you follow after the plants.
"Thus he conforms to the plants, for as an embryo you are born again"—for he is indeed born again as an embryo;
"an embryo of these plants, an embryo of the trees, an embryo of every being, O Agni, an embryo of the waters"—thereby he makes him the embryo of this entire universe. 6.8.2. [5]
He consumes it with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus consumes it: first with one, then with two; or else first with two, then with one.
Twice he consumes it; thus, with those animals that have two feet, he thereby causes him to consume it. Then he takes it away.
That which is here related to Agni, he thereby generates from the waters; for by means of this [verse], medicine is indeed produced.

By this very [verse] he prepares it; having propitiated it with ashes, he says, "Agni, together with the waters and the earth, [prepares] the womb," for he is indeed propitiated by the ashes and becomes [united] with the waters and the earth. Having been united with his mothers, he says, "Thou, full of light, hast settled again," meaning, having come together with his mothers, thou, full of light, hast settled again.
"Having returned to this seat again with vigor and wealth"—by this he means, "return to me with all of that.
He takes [the earth] up with four [verses]. Thus, by means of those animals which have four feet, he thereby gathers this [earth]; moreover, it is food.
Verily, cattle are food; it is with food that he thus equips him. He pours it down three times; that makes seven. The fire-altar consists of seven layers;
there are seven seasons in a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become. 6.8.2. [8]

Having taken up some ashes and returned, he scatters them into the fire-pan and stands worshipping it with two verses addressed to Agni. For when one carries the fire into the water, he does what is improper; he thus makes amends to that very fire for the sake of non-injury. With two verses addressed to Agni...
Thus he denies this by means of two verses addressed to Agni, so that Agni may understand this speech of his:
"O youngest one, heed this speech of mine!"—
thus, "Heed this speech of mine."
"O youngest one"—this refers to him. "Of the most bountiful, of the offered, O self-dependent one"—this means "of the most abundant, of the offered, O self-dependent one.
"One reviles, another praises"—one reviles, while another praises.
"I, a worshipper, praise thy body, O Agni"—this means "I, as a worshipper, praise thy body, O Agni. "Be thou a liberal patron, a giver of wealth."
"O Lord of Wealth, O Giver of Wealth, keep those who hate us away from us"—by saying this, he prays that he may indeed keep those who hate him away from him.
He worships with two verses, one in the *gāyatrī* metre and one in the *triṣṭubh* metre; the significance of this has already been explained.
There are nine of these [verses].
The nine directions are Agni; the nine vital breaths are Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. 6.8.2. [11] Then he performs the expiation.
Verily, he establishes this [fire] for the sake of all desires. Whatever of his desires is cut off here when water is poured into the fire, that he thereby continues and joins together.
He performs both expiations; the significance of those two which are performed when the fire has gone out has already been explained. 6.8.2. [12]
These become ten. The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; Agni is the *virāj*. There are ten directions; Agni is the directions. There are ten vital breaths; Agni is the vital breaths.
As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become.
